Live injury updates

Nico Collins has been ruled out for the Houston Texans' Week 2 game against the Cincinnati Bengals. The wide receiver suffered a hamstring injury during Wednesday's practice and he was not on the field Friday as the team continued preparations.

According to KPRC2's Aaron Wilson, Collins is dealing with a Grade 1 hamstring strain.

Collins isn't the only wide receiver at risk of missing Week 2. Both Lamar Jackson and Justin Herbert each could be without key weapons on Sunday.

In Baltimore, Ravens wideout Zay Flowers is doubtful after leaving Week 1 with a hamstring injury. That issue had kept him out of practice all week after head coach Jesse Minter had labeled him day-to-day, but he was back on the field on Friday. Jackson will already not have Ja'Kobi Lane as a target after the rookie was placed on injured reserve following wrist surgery.

Ladd McConkey was at Los Angeles Chargers' practice on Thursday, but working off to the side. The wide receiver suffered a rib injury during their Week 1 loss to the Arizona Cardinals and was also said to be day-to-day. He did take the field for Friday's practice, but the Chargers have ruled him "questionable" for Sunday's game.

Cooper Rush will start again for the Atlanta Falcons with Jack Strand backing him up. Tua Tagovailoa is not fully recovered from the oblique injury that kept him from playing in Week 1 and Michael Penix Jr. (ACL) is "close" to returning, but has been ruled out.

Other Week 2 injuries to monitor:

  • Kyler Murray was ruled out by the Minnesota Vikings after suffering a concussion in Week 1 against the Green Bay Packers. Carson Wentz will get the start against the Chicago Bears. Head coach Kevin O'Connell expects Murray to clear protocol next week.

  • New England Patriots running back TreVeyon Henderson (ankle) will play Week 2 against the Steelers, he told reporters on Thursday. Henderson missed the opening game with an ankle injury suffered during training camp.

  • Same goes for New Orleans Saints back Alvin Kamara. The veteran sat out Week 1 with a knee sprain, but also declared himself fit to play against the Ravens this week. "I'm going," Kamara said. "If it wasn't right, I wouldn't be in. I feel great, moving well, really no limitations. I feel good."

  • Brock Bowers is doubtful for Sunday's game the Chargers, but he is expected to take part in pregame warmup and will be considered a gametime decision. The tight end had surgery to repair his meniscus and was reportedly set to miss 1-2 games after sitting out the opener. He was on the field for Friday's practice.

item.title: College Players to Watch: Week 2
item.description: With Week 1 over, here are some college players to keep your eyes on for Week 2 and why they could matter to the Saints
item.content:encoded:
The Saints showed on Sunday that there are still some areas they need to improve. Here are some college prospects to keep an eye on going into the Week 2 matchup who could be making major strides early this football season.

DB is a position where you can never have enough talent. KJ Bolden is a name that should always stay on the radar. This nickel/safety is very versatile and is a key contributor in a Kirby Smart defense, so he should transition into the NFL very well. Bolden and the Bulldogs will be playing against Arkansas at 11 a.m. on Saturday.

Tae Johnson is another safety with size and range. Johnson plays for Notre Dame and will be facing off against Michigan State on Saturday night at 6:30 p.m.

Ty Benefield is a fast-rising safety at LSU. He is very experienced, but he is also a first-off-the-bus type of defender. Not only does he look the part, but he can play multiple positions across the secondary. He can play down in the box, deep off the ball or even in the slot. Benefield will be in Oxford taking on the Rebels on Saturday at 6:30 p.m.

Linebacker is another position group on the defense that needs to be watched as well.

Sammy Brown is a name that should be remembered. Brown is a physically gifted linebacker who can cover every single blade of grass and does not have to come off the field on third downs. Brown will be playing against North Carolina on Saturday at 11 a.m.

Chris Cole is another name to watch for Georgia. Who wouldn’t want a linebacker coming out of Georgia? Cole has length at the position and can affect the passer in pass-rushing situations, but he’s not just a pass rusher. He can still play traditional linebacker as well. Georgia is playing Arkansas, so you can get a two-for-one by watching this game.

We talked about cornerback last week and went over Leonard Moore. Here are two other names to watch out for.

Ellis Robinson IV, yes, another Georgia Bulldog. Robinson is a long, rangy, athletic corner. He can hold his own in press-man situations and cover zones very well. Again, he plays in a Kirby Smart defense.

Kelley Jones at Mississippi State is probably the best player on the defense, if not the team. His frame and athleticism started to showcase themselves near the end of last season, and if he follows that up with another good year, expect him to shoot up NFL Draft boards. Jones will have a good matchup on Saturday against South Carolina with Nyck Harbor and LaNorris Sellers at 3:15 p.m.

The offensive line did not look that good in the game against Detroit, so here are two names to watch for this week.

Trevor Goosby and Jordan Seaton are both star tackles with elite size and athleticism who are also great pass protectors. Goosby plays for Texas, and the Longhorns will be playing against UTSA on Saturday at 7 p.m. Seaton plays for LSU and will be with Benefield in Oxford facing off against the Rebels at 6:30 p.m. on Saturday.

What are some other names you’re keeping your eyes on this weekend?

Share your thoughts in the comments below.

item.title: Broncos vs. Jaguars: 3 Players to Watch in Week 2
item.description: These three players need to perform well for the Denver Broncos to secure a victory against the Jacksonville Jaguars.
item.content:encoded:
The Denver Broncos looked absolutely dreadful in their Week 1 loss to the Kansas City Chiefs. Whether it was on offense or defense, nothing seemed to click or go right for them. This weekend, they host the Jacksonville Jaguars who are 1-0 to start the season after beating the Cleveland Browns last Sunday. In order for the Broncos to have a shot at defeating the Jaguars, these three players have to perform at a high level.

J.K. Dobbins — Running Back

Offensive Coordinator Davis Webb opted with the bold strategy of barely running the ball on the road at Arrowhead on Monday Night Football. That put an immense amount of pressure on Bo Nix, who wound up struggling and having one of his worst games of his career. This Sunday, establishing the run has to be a focal point of their offensive plans.

The Jaguars boast a strong defensive line that is extremely good stopping the run. However, the Broncos have to try and get their ground game going if they want any chance at winning on Sunday. J.K. Dobbins was out due to injury in last year’s loss against Jacksonville.

Denver spent all offseason trying to revitalize and improve their rushing attack—let’s see them try and enforce that. If RJ Harvey is dinged up and not available to go due to a hamstring issue, rookie running back Jonah Coleman should see his first carries of the regular season.

Courtland Sutton — Wide Receiver

Last week against the Chiefs, I noted Jaylen Waddle as a player that needed to have a huge game. Unfortunately, Denver’s prized trade acquisition had one catch for two yards. That’s simply unacceptable. Courtland Sutton also failed to make an impact and had just two catches for 11 yards.

This week, Sutton has to rise to the occasion and make an impact in the Broncos’ passing game. In last year’s matchup, Sutton led the Broncos with six receptions for 86 yards and a touchdown. He will have to be at his best to give Denver a chance to win.

Whether it’s a touchdown catch or reverting back to form and being a chain-moving machine, the receiver corps elder statesman has to play at a high level. Of course, that also means Bo Nix has to do a better job at quarterback. The Broncos’ aerial attack can’t be flat for the second game in a row. Enough of the slow starts.

Alex Singleton — Linebacker

Truth be told, you could insert almost any player on defense as someone to watch and hope they improve drastically after what happened against the Chiefs. The defensive line was overmatched, the edge rushers failed to get adequate pressure, and several members of the Broncos’ secondary had a rough outing.

For Sunday’s game against the Jaguars, I’m choosing inside linebacker Alex Singleton. His agent went to social media to blast fans and writers for criticizing the team. After the game, Singleton’s comments rubbed a lot of folks across Broncos Country the wrong way. I expect team captains to be more accountable than that.

Liam Coen loves to diversify his personnel groupings, work in a lot of motion, and do whatever it’s necessary to try and confuse opposing defenses pre-snap. He also likes to utilize running backs in the passing game. I think that will pose a challenge for Singleton who has struggled with the latter on more than one occasion.

Will he rise up to the challenge and play better on Sunday? You’ll just have to tune in and find out.

item.title: Important Cowboys vs Commanders storylines on Sunday
item.description: What do you think is the biggest storyline entering Sunday?
item.content:encoded:
I don’t think anyone expected things to go the way they did in the Dallas Cowboys vs. New York Giants game. Without dwelling too much on a game in the rearview mirror, the Dallas defense caught many by surprise considering the overhaul over the offseason. Guys like Jalen Thompson, Rashan Gary, and Caleb Downs were supposed to usher in something different.

Unfortunately, it was more of the same.

Here’s the good news. It was Week 1. The Cowboys still have 16 regular-season games left, and they have plenty of time to turn things around. They have to do it in a must-win way this week against the Washington Commanders.

Here are five points to watch for as the game kicks off on Sunday.

First point: More of the same?

Heading into their matchup with the Giants, one of last week’s five points was limiting Jaxson Dart in the running game. The Cowboys had 54 yards on the ground to Dart, averaging almost five yards per carry. Dart’s ability to scramble kept Dallas’ defense on the field, which we all know how that went.

The Cowboys have another quarterback coming up on Sunday who can hurt them with his legs: Jayden Daniels. Last week against the Philadelphia Eagles, Daniels didn’t run for as many yards as Dart did in Dallas, but he was an effective runner when he had the opportunity or needed to make a play. He had five carries for 31 yards, averaging over six yards every time he would run.

Dallas needs to make sure last week’s mistake doesn’t happen again, because it’ll lead to more of the same, with the Commanders extending drives and keeping the Cowboys offense on the sidelines.

Second point: The terror twins or the DeVille twins

Somehow, someway, the Cowboys need to get CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens the ball early and often against the Commanders. Brian Schottenheimer has talked about wanting to run the ball and set the tone, but the team’s real playmakers are on the outside.

On a great day, both wideouts can have over 100 yards each and be a terror to opposing defenses. Against the Giants, it just seemed like Pickens and Prescott weren’t always on the same page, and we’ve seen how Lamb can take time to get going if things don’t go his way early in a game.

The best version of Lamb and Pickens earned them the nickname “the terror twins.” That version of the duo needs to be on display vs. the Commanders’ smaller cornerbacks. Last year against the Commanders at AT&T Stadium, Lamb went for 110 receiving yards and Pickens had 85. Both players averaged over 20 yards per catch. What we don’t need to see are the DeVille twins, which, if anyone has seen the show Rugrats, you know what I’m talking about.

Third point: A rookie DC in DC

The Commanders have the same question at defensive coordinator as the Cowboys do: Is this moment too big for them? Head coach Dan Quinn went out and hired two first-time coordinators on both sides of the ball this offseason, which could make him look like a genius or get him fired.

Washington’s DC should be a familiar name to Cowboys fans since he was in the running for the same position with Dallas: Daronte Jones. He spent most of his coaching career with the Minnesota Vikings and learned under Brian Flores over the last three seasons. Unlike Christian Parker, Jones was actually a defensive coordinator in college in 2021 for LSU. That was his only season holding the position.

Against the Eagles, the Commanders defense looked good and got the Philly offense out of rhythm on multiple drives. However, a few explosive plays happened where it looked like the secondary didn’t know what was going on (sound familiar).

It’ll be interesting to see the storylines coming out of the game because one of these teams will be 0-2, with a ton of questions surrounding their first-time defensive coordinators and whether they were the right guys for the job.

Fourth point: Reading between the linebackers

Before offseason training and the NFL draft, the Cowboys’ linebacking corps was seen as a glaring need, even with Jaishawn Barham and Dee Winters coming aboard. DeMarvion Overshown’s health was a question, and Dallas needed to keep developing second-year pro Shemar James.

As time went on, the questions around linebacker seemed to shift towards the pass rush and secondary. We should have stuck with our first instincts. With Overshown leaving Week 1 with a hamstring injury that could cost him one to two weeks, the Cowboys linebacker room looks even thinner heading into Week 2.

Barham could be called upon as the next man up with green-dot responsibilities, but with growing concerns about the defense’s ability to communicate calls properly, should a rookie be trusted to make the right calls? Dallas has Curtis Robinson and Justin Barron on the practice squad and could elevate one of them to the active roster for Sunday, but they aren’t on the same level as Overshown to fill the void.

The Cowboys were impressed by what they saw from Barham all offseason and in the first preseason game. If that player is still there, which he should be, the Dallas defense will need him in a big way this weekend.

Fifth point: Kicking and screaming

No need to panic; this is an under-the-radar point my colleague RJ Ochoa brought up on Twitter.

Dating back to last season, Dallas Cowboys kicker Brandon Aubrey has now missed a kick of some kind (field goal or extra point) in 3 straight games.

This is the first time in his career he has a 3-game streak of such kind.

Aubrey is one of, if not the best, kickers in the NFL. However, if the defense struggles to start the season and the offense needs to score as many points as possible in their opportunities, missing kicks can’t happen. Questions lingered about the special teams unit’s performance last year under Nick Sorensen, and doubt remains about his return this offseason.

Sorensen stuck around, and so far, after one game, the special teams unit has not looked any better in year two. Aubrey signed a historic deal this offseason, and deservedly so. But if he starts missing critical kicks in games that could come down to three points, it could raise alarm bells about what’s happened to one of the league’s most clutch kickers.

item.title: Dolphins’ Chop Robinson out for Sunday vs. 49ers
item.description: Miami will be without one of its top pass rushers as the defense looks for answers against the 49ers.
item.content:encoded:
After being downgraded on Thursday’s injury report following a concussion, Dolphins’ edge rusher Chop Robinson has officially been ruled out ahead of Sunday afternoon’s game against the San Francisco 49ers.

Dolphins coach Jeff Hafley said Robinson suffered the concussion during Wednesday’s practice. It is Robinson’s third concussion within the last year.

Also ruled out of the game was linebacker Ronnie Harrison, Jr. Primarily a special teams player in Week 1, Harrison has been dealing with a hamstring injury that kept him from practicing all week.

With Robinson sidelined, Josh Uche, Malik Herring, Robert Beal Jr., and potentially Clelin Ferrell, who is currently on the practice squad, are all candidates to see increased workloads. Hafley could also continue deploying defensive tackle Zeek Biggers on the edge, as he did during last Sunday’s loss to the Raiders.

Miami’s injury report also listed long snapper Tucker Addington as questionable for the game. Addington injured his shoulder in Week 1 but played through the rest of the game.

The 49ers’ side of the injury report included officially ruling out wide receiver De’Zhaun Stribling who did not practice throughout the week with an ankle injury. as well as designating running back Kaelon Black and kicker Eddy Pineiro as questionable. Black was limited in practice on Thursday and Friday after sustaining a groin injury. Pineiro did not practice all week due to an illness.

The Dolphins and 49ers kickoff on Sunday at 4:25 p.m. Eastern.

item.title: Hollywood Brown: I don't know if chances will come, I just have to work
item.description: Wide receiver Hollywood Brown was active for the Eagles' Week 1 game against the Commanders, but he never got on the field during the 24-22 win.
item.content:encoded:
Wide receiver Hollywood Brown was active for the Eagles' Week 1 game against the Commanders, but he never got on the field during the 24-22 win.

Brown said this week that there were "no conversations" with coaches leading up to the game about his role. Head coach Nick Sirianni said on Monday that they "obviously want to get him into the football game because his speed is real," but that the rotations "just didn't work out that way" last Sunday.

Brown said he is unsure if anything will change against the Titans this week, but that he'll work to be ready for any opportunity that might come his way.

“That I don’t know,” Brown said, via Ryan Novozinsky of the Philadelphia Inquirer. “I just got to come to work. If it do, it do. If it don’t, it don’t.”

Brown was added to Friday's injury report as a full participant with a hamstring injury, but has no injury designation for Sunday. Whether that means he'll be on the field remains up in the air.

item.title: Arizona Cardinals offensive and defensive interior limited heading into Sunday
item.description: Arizona Cardinals injury report littered with starters.
item.content:encoded:
The Arizona Cardinals need “questionable” to just be posturing on Sunday.

It’s not that a win would be impossible without some of these guys, maybe one on offense and one on defense, but it will be much, much harder.

The Arizona Cardinals will again be without Garrett Williams, which is bad enough considering they are going up against Jaxon Smith-Njigba, but you now have both starting guards questionable and both nose tackles questionable for Sunday.

Isaiah Adams, who missed game one has been limited with a knee issue all week, while Isaac Seumalo popped up with a shoulder injury on Wednesday and was either out or limited all week as well.

Then you have Andrew Billings who missed game one and has been limited this week, while the star of the game one win Roy Lopez, had a groin issue come up and made him miss Wednesday and be limited today.

Let’s just hope everyone is healthy. Or at least half of each side of the ball, for Sunday.

Sometimes, the best run defense can be getting out to a lead on offense and forcing the opposition to become one-dimensional. There was certainly an element of that in Week 1, when the hosts kept the ball on the ground 38 times compared to the visitors’ 15. Still, Kansas City did a nice job bottling up starting Broncos halfback J.K. Dobbins to the tune of 36 yards.

After ranking 13th in EPA per rush given up in 2025 (-0.06, per SumerSports), that slotting was fourth after a week of 2026 play thanks to an EPA/rush allowance of -0.19. The three-time NFL Defensive Player of the Year would make his return at SoFi Stadium, where he previously played his home games and helped lead the Rams to a Super Bowl win over the Cincinnati Bengals in February 2022.

“That’s the plan,” Donald said when asked if he’ll play against the Giants. “That’s all of our plan. We’ll have a conversation to figure it out, but I’m feeling really good. I feel a lot better now that I have more practices under my belt as opposed to one.”

Collins was healthy to start Wednesday’s practice but tweaked a hamstring later in the session. The injury doesn’t appear to be long term. Collins met with team doctors after Wednesday’s practice and the injury isn’t believed to be “serious,” a source told ESPN’s Adam Schefter.

The Texans’ official injury report listed Collins as limited in Wednesday’s practice due to the injury. He was listed as a nonparticipant in Thursday’s and Friday’s practice.

Bowers underwent surgery to trim his meniscus last week, which sidelined him for the Raiders’ Week 1 win over the Miami Dolphins. Kubiak said earlier this week that Bowers was considered “day-to-day” after the surgery. The tight end did not practice on Wednesday or Thursday.

item.content:encoded:
In Week 2 of 2026 our Indianapolis Colts will hit the road to take on the Kansas City Chiefs. Knowing the party was headed to KC, I sat down with Maurice Elston of Arrowhead Pride, SB Nation’s Chiefs blog. You can find him on Twitter @MrMauriceElston. We swapped questions and answers about both the Chiefs and Colts and what follows is what I’ve learned about this week’s opponent.

You can find my answers to his questions here.

Chris Shepherd: Based on Week 1, if you were an offensive coordinator tasked with creating a game plan to attack the Chiefs’ defense, what would your plan look like? What areas of the field would you attack, what weaknesses would you target and how would you try to beat this Chiefs defense?

Maurice Elston:I would do anything possible to force Kansas City’s linebackers—primarily Nick Bolton—to cover in space or match up one-on-one. Bolton is an excellent run defender and the commander of the Chiefs’ defense, but operating in coverage over a large area is not his greatest strength.

I would attack the middle of the field with tight ends and running backs, using motion and different formations to create favorable matchups against the linebackers. The Colts have a tight end in Tyler Warren who is capable of presenting that type of problem. Getting Warren matched against Bolton or another linebacker in space could give Indianapolis an opportunity to consistently move the football.

Chris Shepherd: In Week 1, Colts fans watched in horror as the Ravens moved Zay Flowers all over the field to exploit favorable matchups that the discombobulated Colts secondary never figured out how to adjust to. Do you think the Chiefs will try to exploit those same issues, and if so, who will Andy Reid and Eric Bieniemy slot into the Zay Flowers role for Kansas City?

Maurice Elston: I don’t believe the Chiefs will copy Baltimore’s strategy exactly because Kansas City doesn’t have to lean on one receiver the way the Ravens leaned on Flowers. I absolutely expect Andy Reid and Eric Bieniemy to test the same communication problems Indianapolis experienced in Week 1, but they will likely do it with several different players.

The Chiefs can use motion, shifts and formations to create favorable matchups for Rashee Rice, Xavier Worthy, Travis Kelce and Kenneth Walker III. Instead of putting one player in the Flowers role, Kansas City can force the Colts to identify and communicate against multiple threats before the snap. That unpredictability could make the assignment even more difficult for Indianapolis’ secondary.

Chris Shepherd: In Week 1, Patrick Mahomes made his return after recovering from last season’s torn ACL. He completed 15 of 27 passes for 184 yards, two touchdowns and an interception. Did Mahomes look like the Patrick of old? Was he still the player who can take over games, or will he need some time to regain that form?

Maurice Elston:I wouldn’t say Mahomes completely looked like his old self, but he did look healthy—and that was the most important thing Kansas City needed to see.

Mahomes demonstrated that his knee is fine, he can still scramble and he remains capable of making plays outside the pocket. From a passing standpoint, however, there was some understandable rust. He opened the game completing only two of his first 12 attempts and missed a few routine throws that we normally see him make.

He eventually settled down and completed 13 of his final 15 attempts, including two touchdown passes. Because he couldn’t participate in his normal offseason routine and did not play during the preseason, some early rust should have been expected. He may not be completely back to his old form yet, but the second half showed that he is getting there.

Chris Shepherd: Can you give me one player on offense and one on defense whom Colts fans might not be familiar with but who you expect to make an impact Sunday night?

Maurice Elston:Offensively, I would watch rookie wide receiver Cyrus Allen. He became one of the Chiefs’ most talked-about young players during training camp and the preseason. Allen received only one target and did not record a catch in Week 1, but I expect Kansas City to begin incorporating him into the offense.

In my opinion, Allen may already be the best pure route runner in the Chiefs’ wide receiver room. His ability to separate could become especially valuable against the man-to-man coverage Kansas City’s receivers have consistently faced.

Defensively, I’ll go with L’Jarius Sneed. It may seem strange to call Sneed an under-the-radar player considering what he has accomplished, but much of the attention surrounding Kansas City’s secondary has focused on young outside cornerbacks Mansoor Delane and Nohl Williams.

Sneed’s return to the slot gives Steve Spagnuolo a trusted defender who can cover, blitz and handle several different assignments. Having someone Spagnuolo trusts to lock down the slot changes what the Chiefs can do schematically, making Sneed an important piece of this defense even if he isn’t receiving the most attention.

Chris Shepherd: How do you predict this game will play out? What does each team do well, where will they struggle and what is the final score?

Maurice Elston: I expect the Chiefs to win, although I don’t anticipate the margin being as large as it was against Denver.

Indianapolis’ best path to keeping the game close is through Jonathan Taylor and Tyler Warren. The Colts must remain committed to Taylor, stay ahead of the chains and use Warren to attack Kansas City’s linebackers and safeties in coverage. There is no completely stopping Taylor because he is too talented, but if the Chiefs can contain him enough to force Indianapolis into third-and-long situations, Kansas City’s pass rush and pressure packages can take control.

For the Colts defensively, the challenge will be handling Kansas City’s motion, personnel groupings and improved running game without experiencing the communication breakdowns that hurt them against Baltimore. If those problems continue, Reid and Bieniemy will find ways to exploit them.

I believe Indianapolis keeps the game competitive for a while, but Kansas City eventually creates some separation and wins 24-14.

I can’t thank Maurice enough for answering this week’s questions. Make sure you head over to Arrowhead Pride and @MrMauriceElston on Twitter to check out his work.

As always, go Colts.

item.title: 3 X-Factors for the Browns clash with the Buccaneers in Week 2
item.description: Week 2’s Cleveland Browns versus TB Bucs is not just about Baker Mayfield, Deshaun Watson. A few X-Factors also matter
item.content:encoded:
The Cleveland Browns will try to finish their two-game Florida road trip on a positive note as the team will travel to Tampa Bay to play the Buccaneers this Sunday. For the Browns, it’s all about trying to bounce back after a rough season opener against the Jacksonville Jaguars. As a collective, the Browns didn’t play well at all, and it doesn’t get much easier as they will play a Buccaneers team that will have a highly motivated quarterback in Baker Mayfield.

Here are three X-Factors for Browns vs Bucs in Week 2:

Zac Robinson vs Mike Rutenberg

In terms of debuts for coordinators in new situations, both Zac Robinson and Mike Rutenberg would’ve like to have done things differently. However, if people don’t know by now, Rutenberg and Robinson have history. Both Robinson and Rutenberg were with the Atlanta Falcons last year under former Falcons head coach Raheem Morris (who is now the San Francisco 49ers defensive coordinator). Robinson was the offensive coordinator and Rutenberg was the defensive passing game coordinator.

Robinson had his issues against the Cincinnati Bengals, mainly in terms of communication when it came to relaying the plays, but he called a somewhat competent game. Rutenberg, on the other hand, struggled. The Browns defense spent more time playing zone coverage rather than man coverage, which led to frequent coverage busts. The players have to execute, but the defensive coordinator has to put the players in better situations.

Familiarity is well known between the two, but Rutenberg has to call a better game defensively and make life difficult for Tampa Bay’s offense.

Browns DBs vs Bucs WRs

In terms of matchups, this one will be one to monitor. Browns cornerback Denzel Ward was the only cornerback that played well last week against the Jacksonville Jaguars. Cornerback Myles Harden struggled mightily, while Tyson Campbell’s performance wasn’t nearly as poor as Harden’s; it wasn’t great.

This week doesn’t get any easier. Ward will likely be matched up with Buccaneers wide receiver Emeka Egbuka, Campbell will likely be tasked against Jalen McMillan or rookie Ted Hurst, Myles Harden will be tasked against Chris Godwin. It’s hard to imagine the secondary playing any worse than they did last week but the Bucs have versatility in the wide receiver room.

Campbell’s questionable status for the game could create other issues.

It’s possible that the cornerbacks will have to play more zone due to the lack of a consistent pass rush. It’s not necessarily ideal, but due to the pass rush not being there, they might not have a choice.

Cleveland Defensive Line vs Tampa’s Offensive Line

By the Browns standards, their defensive line didn’t perform to the level that they are capable of in Week 1.

The pass rush was nonexistent, and the run defense was questionable at best. Tampa’s offensive line had an uneven performance, as the pass blocking wasn’t up to standard, but the run blocking was solid in their opening contest. As for the Browns, the pass rush needs to be better. It’s simple as that. Pressure was going to fall off after the team traded away Myles Garrett; it’s the reality of the situation. However, Jared Verse, who they traded for in the Garrett deal, wasn’t the best defensive lineman for the Browns that day. That was Mason Graham.

Aside from quarterback play, the game will be determined in the trenches, and both units (who had lackluster debuts) will look for redemption this week.

item.title: The Good, The Bad, and The Ugly: Wake Forest Demon Deacons 2026 Edition
item.description: Miami was rolling then…..WHAT HAPPENED?!
item.content:encoded:
Another game, another victory for the Canes! On Friday night, your Miami Hurricanes continued the ACC schedule, traveling to Winston-Salem, NC to play, and beat, the Wake Forest Demon Deacons 33-20.

Craig T. Smith has your game recap:

AND Mike Schiffman is back with the 3 stars of the game:

And with no further ado, let’s get into this edition of The Good, The Bad, and The Ugly:

The Good

  • A win! I will never take this for granted.
  • QB Darian Mensah. 30/34 passing, 220 yards, 3 touchdowns, 0 interceptions
  • Mensah’s cumulative stats this year: 71/79 passing, 90% completions, 873 yards, 11 touchdowns, 0 interceptions.
  • WR Malachi Toney. 12 catches for 114 yards and a touchdown.
  • Toney’s cumulative stats: 28 catches for 444 yards and 5 touchdowns.
  • RB Mark Fletcher Jr. 16 carries for 85 yards and a touchdown.
  • S J.J. Dunnigan. 8 tackles, 3 QB hurries, and another great game from my favorite player.
  • CB Ethan O’Connor. 8 tackles, solid coverage, and the game-winning interception. Bravo.
  • The defensive line. EDGEs Armondo Blount, Marquise Lightfoot, and Damon Wilson II finally made their presence felt. DTs Justin Scott and Ahmad Moten Sr. also played very very well.
  • In total, the DL combined for 13 tackles, 3 sacks, and 3.5 TFLs. Oh, and forced 3 holding penalties, which could have easily been tripled. There was pressure all day long, and solid run defense as well. It wasn’t perfect, but this was a big step forward for the defensive line.
  • Miami walking 92 yards down the field in 14 plays to score on the first drive of the game. Great choices from Mensah, solid play all around, and in the end, a touchdown. That’ll work.
  • The opening drive, in EPA chart form:
  • That drive ended with this 9-yard touchdown pass from Mensah to WR Joshua Moore.
  • Mark Fletcher Jr. running dudes over!!!!!! Or, in the words of Marshawn Lynch: RUN THRU A MUFUCKA’S FACE!!!!!
  • Mensah to TE Elija Lofton for a 21 yard score. Y-leak. Wide open. Easy as you like. (and look at Mensah’s opening stats after 2 drives. LOL my goodness)
  • EDGE Damon Wilson II with his first sack as a Hurricane!
  • LB Mo Toure with a MASSIVE hit to force a fumble, which would have been Miami’s first takeaway of the year but there was a penalty away from the ball.
  • CB Ethan O’Connor called game.
  • 295 yards of offense in the first half
  • Scoring touchdowns on the first 3 drives of the night.
  • Scoring on 5 of our first 6 offensive drives.
  • Forcing Wake Forest into 3-and-outs on their final 4 first half drives.
  • Forcing Wake Forest’s final 3 drives to end as follows: downs at the Miami 14, Downs at the Wake 42, and an interception from the Miami 22.
  • Held Wake to 4/13 on 3rd down
  • Held Wake to 1/3 on 4th down
  • Held Wake to 1.4 yards per rush
  • 158 yards rushing
  • 5.6 yards per play
  • 4.6 yards per rush
  • 68 total plays of offense
  • 4-4 scoring in the redzone (all touchdowns)
  • 33:24 time of possession
  • 5 TFLs
  • 3 sacks
  • 9 QB hurries
  • 1 takeaway — O’Connor’s interception
  • A solid win by the advanced stats, too

The Bad

  • Allowed 20 first downs
  • Allowed 10.8 yards per completion
  • Allowed 3 TFLs
  • Allowed 2 sacks
  • Only 7.3 yards per completion
  • 5/13 on 3rd down
  • 1 for the final 8 on 3rd down
  • Mensah 220 yards on 30 completions? Woof.
  • I know Wake Forest was trying to play zone to take away the super explosive plays….but they went to man-to-man schemes in the 2nd half and Miami did nothing against them. Can’t have that. That’s bad.
  • Losing the second half 13-9
  • No Jordan Lyle, despite him being dressed for the game, and Miami losing the top 2 backs on the depth chart. His de-facto suspension continues.

The Ugly

  • 7 penalties for 75 yards. Nowhere NEAR good enough.
  • Whatever the FUCK happened after we went up 31-7. Kill it with fire.
  • No seriously, I’m trying to understand what happened. Miami’s offense was walking up and down the field, then did less than nothing on the final 6 drives of the game. Truly baffling.
  • After going up 31-7, these were Miami’s next 4 drives:
  • And the next drive after those 4? 4 plays, 6 yards, no first downs, and a blocked FG from 54 yards. TRULY terrible stuff.
  • Injuries. Injuries. And more injuries. Seriously, somebody reset the sliders or something.
  • ALL the missed sacks on Gio Lopez. Credit to him for being a tough player and elusive to a point, but there were a lot of bad plays on Miami’s part that enabled him to extend plays.
  • Cam Pruitt with a holding penalty on the opening kick return of the game. C’mon man.
  • Mark Fletcher Jr. with a block in the back on an early screen to Daylyn Upshaw. Gotta play clean!
  • ‘twas a questionable call
  • DT Ahmad Moten Sr. leaving the game early with a left shoulder injury. You truly hate to see it. Damnit.
  • DL Armondo Blount called for a weak roughing the passer to gift Wake Forest extra yards on top of a completion.
  • Miami’s defense gave up their first touchdown of the year on Wake’s first drive.
  • Again, whatever that was after Miami went up 31-7. I’m very upset by the deterioration of the offense, and the penalties that allowed Wake to move down the field and score on the defense.
  • RB Marty Brown suffering what the broadcast called a “gruesome” knee injury on a 32 yard run midway through the 2nd quarter. Brown is Miami’s Swiss Army Knife backup RB. Losing him would hurt the depth, but present opportunities for others. Still, you HATE to see injuries. UGH.
  • This is the play where Brown sustained his injury
  • TE Elija Lofton went down with a left leg (ankle?) injury late in the 2nd quarter. TURN OFF INJURIES.
  • RB Mark Fletcher Jr. missing/not attempting a block vs the blitz, leading to a sack of Darian Mensah. Great player, ugly play
  • EDGE Damon Wilson II called for roughing the passer to negate Miami’s first takeaway of the year, a forced fumble my LB Mo Toure on a MASSIVE hit against the Wake RB.
  • Wake Forest had a guy ALL ALONE on 4th and 5. It was incomplete, but had they seen this, it’s a touchdown. Bottom of the picture below, just above the “33” on the scorebug.
  • I’m just…..disappointed. The lack of focus. The penalties. The stagnation on offense. The PENALTIES. The missed sacks. The injuries. THE PENALTIES. I know we won by 2 touchdowns but this was nowhere near good enough.

Team Grades

Offense: First 6 drives: A+; Last 6 drives: F-

Truly a Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde performance. Miami had a plan and answers for Wake’s zone scheme to be methodical, consistent, slightly explosive, and go up and down the field easily to build a 31-7 lead.

And then invasion of the body snatchers happened and Miami’s offense went into a shell, and had 4 consecutive 3-and-outs and a 4 play drive that ended with a blocked FG before the final drive where they FINALLY converted a 1st down to secure the victory.

I know there were injuries, but Miami has too much talent for this to happen on offense. Mensah looked dinged up, but I’m sure Miami won’t say he was. Malachi Toney was on a pitch count after straining his abdominals stretching for a catch late in the second quarter. STILL, the fact that Miami’s offense turned into…..whatever it was that we watched after the 1st drive of the second half is unacceptable. Full stop.

Defense: C-

Defensive line actually showed a pulse which is great. But there were issues with Mo Toure and Omar Thornton, both players who have been questioned for their coverage abilities, giving up touchdowns on the same slot fade concept. And there were a metric ton of missed tackles, SPECIFICALLY sack opportunities on Lopez. Yes, the defense was able to step up and get stops late in the game when they were needed, yes they were able to get stops early, but there is still MUCH to be desired here.

Special Teams: F-

Penalty on the opening kick return of the game. Good punting when we used it but we used it too much for my liking, especially given the early production from the offense. Add in a missed/blocked FG, and yeah, that isn’t a showing anybody is excited about.

Coaching: D

I almost feel like Mario Cristobal’s continual statements about middling teams being better than they are was a self fulfilling prophecy tonight. Wake is FINE, but Miami is a clear class better than them…..or was for 34 minutes of the game. Then, Miami went into a shell, let Wake hang around, and that just wasn’t at all necessary.

Let me be clear: it wasn’t the INTENT of the coaching staff or offense to play poorly and let Wake hang around, but it felt like that was the impact.

Operationally, the offense played a clean game. The only offensive penalty was a questionable block in the back call on Mark Fletcher Jr. And, for the first 34 minutes of the game, the offense was unstoppable. But then there were missed blocks. And *VERY* conservative play calls (all the screens), and some poor play (WOOF, offensive line), and things grinded to a halt. Dawson had answers, then didn’t. And he has to find something to settle the team and get a first down — which Miami had exactly *ONE* of in the final 27 minutes of the game across 6 possessions. It came 3 plays from the end of the game to give Miami the chance to go to victory formation.

Wake Forest came out to open the game and walked down the field for a 75 yard TD drive to tie the score. In that moment, I said I needed adjustments from DC Corey Hetherman. And I got them. Miami forced 4 consecutive 3-and-outs thereafter and built the big lead we’ve been talking about. I liked the late adjustment to put J.J. Dunnigan at LB and spy Lopez. I liked the unceasing blitzes from the slot (regardless of who was assigned the blitz). I liked the pressure the defensive line got. I liked the variety of players at linebacker, all of whom had some nice moments.

Overall, I thought the defensive scheme was fine, but the inability to complete sacks — seriously, Lopez stepped out of at least 8 MORE sacks than we saw — and ALL. THE. PENALTIES — 6 of Miami’s 7 penalties came on defense — were the issues. Like with the offense, it wasn’t the intent of the coaches to have that performance from the players, but that’s what we got, and it wasn’t good enough.

I’ll admit that this is a harsh grade. But if the standard and goal is to compete for championships, high standards and tough feedback are required.

That’s it for this installment of The Good, The Bad, and The Ugly.

Hop in the comments and let me know your thoughts.

Directional Michigan here we come!

Go Canes

item.title: Big Blue View mailbag: First impressions, retired numbers, penalty reviews
item.description: The mail’s here! This week’s questions, answers about the Giants.
item.content:encoded:
Bob Donnelly asks: It’s great to see the Harbaugh era start with a W and there’s certainly a lot to get excited about.

I’m sure there are some in the glass half empty crowd that will say that the W is nice and John is 1 and 0 in one score games, but there remains some of the latent issues that often derailed this team last year with ball security (4 fumbles , 2 turnover-worth plays) and penalties (#1 penalty yards) leading the list.

As you reflect on the first game performance under Harbaugh what areas concern you most?

Ed says: Bob, absolutely nothing has changed from my preseason evaluation of the Giants. The biggest areas of concern entering the season were cornerback play and defensive line depth. Nothing about Sunday changed that.

Tae Banks was OK. I thought he got pushed off on the touchdown he surrendered. I didn’t think Greg Newsome was that good against the Cowboys, but he was a lot better than Paulson Adebo. Colton Hood still isn’t ready for full-time duty.

DJ Reader and Shelby Harris were fine. When they were replaced by Darius Alexander and C.J. Okoye, Dallas had more success running the ball. If they can find a run-stuffing veteran defensive tackle who can help them get through this season that would be great.

Adam Jacobs asks: I have an offbeat question about the taunting penalty by Javonte Williams. Every penalty that occurs in the field of play is marked at the spot of the foul unless it occurs behind the line of scrimmage. Except the Williams penalty. Why was this enforced after the play was finished, and not from the spot of the foul? I am not sure I have ever seen this before. Do you have any idea how this works?

Ed says: Adam, taunting is treated as a dead-ball foul. Thus, the result of the play stands. The penalty is assessed after the play.

Kölnerbigblue asks: Ed, I know teams can request a review of penalties after the game. Not that it will change any results, can you explain how this process works?

Ed says: The NFL audits every snap during the days after games, looking at calls and non-calls. That is both to assess the performance of the offcials, and to determine discipline when it comes to handing out fines.

NFL teams can send a maximum of 10 plays to the league office each for review, clarification, explanation. Sometimes, the league will admit that a mistake was made. That, though, will not affect an outcome or result in a do-over.

James Pauloski asks: For me, the most amazing statistic from the Cowboys game was that Dallas only had two possessions in the second half. Yes, they scored two touchdowns, but that was it. That seems almost impossible. Did the Giants tie (or set) a record for allowing only two possessions in one half?

Ed says: James, I have been unable to find anything to answer that directly. What I can say is that each team had only seven possessions on Sunday, making 14 total (yes, I can do math!). That is an incredibly low total. There was a 2023 game between the Denver Broncos were there were only 12 possessions, six for each team. It speaks to efficiency by both offenses as there were five drives in the game that took more than six minutes, two of those by the Giants lasting more than eight minutes.

Todd Kuehn asks: Ed, I really like looking at box scores when the game is over because the information and numbers in them are all objective instead of subjective except for two of them. Maybe I’m wrong about that but when you look at the QBR and the RTG for quarterbacks from the Dallas game it seems to me maybe they are subjective. Dart got a really good RTG 134.2 and Prescott only had 84.8. But when you look at the QBR Dart received 81.5 and Prescott had an 89. How can that be? There is no doubt in almost everyone’s mind that Dart outplayed Prescott.

Ed says: Todd, there is no perfect quarterback measuring stick. PFF uses a different methodology than QBR, passer rating, etc. As Tony DelGenio pointed out this week, Pro Football and Sports Network’s ‘Impact Score’ had Dart as the second-highest rated quarterback this week with Prescott 14th. It all depends what they are grading and with they give importance to.

Bottom line is that no matter how Dart was graded by any rating system, it was clear that he played very well and did the things needed for the Giants to win a football game against a good team.

Martin Hand asks: Hi Ed, I just saw an article about Gronkowski and that his number had not been retired yet… It made me think about our situation with Malik and Abdul… Don’t you think it is a bit self-absorbed for an retired individual to think that the number is his and does not belong to the franchise… Players last a few years, whereas the Giants will last forever… I don’t have my heels dug in over this one, but couldn’t help to think about it and wanted to ask you what you thought.

Ed says: Martin, I can’t say I have ever heard that opinion before.

Players don’t decide to retire their numbers. Franchises do that in honor of those players. So, yes, the number belongs to the franchise and that is what the franchise has chosen to do with it.

To be honest, I vehemently disagree with the whole idea of “unretiring” numbers. I think sometimes well-meaning franchises retire too many numbers. Here is the list of Giants’ retired numbers. I think the Giants allowed Malik Nabers to wear the previously retired No. 1 jersey opened a Pandora’s Box that led to the Abdul Carter mess, and that it won’t be the last time there is a situation like that.

Numbers, though, get retired because of a player’s accomplishments. That means something to that player, and to the player’s family. Why should a kid fresh out of college who has done nothing get the number of an all-time franchise great? Because his “brand” revolves around that number? Please.

Jeffrey Jacobs asks: Do you see any scenario where the Giants mange to pry Joey Porter Jr. away from the Steelers, and if so what do you think it would take?

Ed says: Jeffrey, of course there is a scenario where the Giants try to pry Porter Jr. away from the Steelers. I think it is highly unlikely, but if the Giants believe the player is worth the draft capital they would have to surrender and the big price tag they would have to pay him they would try to make it happen.

Spotrac recently posted what their model believes Porter’s price tag would be:

Four years, $110 million would make Porter the seventh-highest paid cornerback in the NFL in terms of average annual value. Is he really worth that kind of money?

Also, the Giants are extremely reluctant to give out contracts of that length. Andrew Thomas and Brian Burns, arguably the two best players on the team not currently on four-year rookie contracts, are the only veteran players with deals of longer than three years.

Are the Giants really going to go there for Porter? Remember, not too far down the road they will have to negotiate long-term deals with Jaxson Dart, Malik Nabers, and Abdul Carter.

As for trade cost in terms of draft capital, I can’t imagine the Steelers being able to drive a hard bargain for Porter if they choose to move him. I am not offering more than an early-Day 3 pick considering the contract I would have to give him.

Marcus Mbow bonus

I was asked many times during the offseason if I knew whether or not second-year offensive tackle Marcus Mbow has put on weight during the offseason. Until Thursday, I couldn’t answer the question because I had not spoken to him at all.

I got a chance to speak with him for a minute in the locker room this week. For all of you obsessed by Mbow’s weight, he put on 15 pounds this offseason and is now around the 320-pound mark.

Submit a question

Have a Giants-related question? E-mail it to bigblueview@gmail.com and it might be featured in our weekly mailbag.

item.title: Previewing the New York Jets’ opposition: Green Bay Packers
item.description: The Jets try for two in a row when they face the Packers on Sunday
item.content:encoded:
The New York Jets welcome the Green Bay Packers for their home opener on Sunday afternoon. While New York is seeking to start 2-0 for the first time since 2015, the Packers are under pressure not to drop to 0-2. They gave up 29 unanswered points as they blew a double-digit lead in their opener against the Vikings.

The Jets won in Green Bay in the last meeting between the teams back in 2022, but that was their first win over the Packers since 2006. However, they lead the all-time series by nine wins to five.

Let’s break down the Packers’ roster going position by position:

Quarterbacks

Packers quarterback Jordan Love is coming off his best season as a full time starter in terms of completion percentage, quarterback rating and touchdown-to-interception ratio. However, he still hasn’t earned pro bowl recognition as he enters his fourth year as a starter.

In game one, Love passed for 387 yards; just two less than his career-high. However, he only completed 50 percent of his passes, was sacked four times, fumbled twice and threw an interception. Can the Jets put some pressure on him?

In the event Love gets knocked out of the game, their backup is a familiar face: former Jets quarterback Tyrod Taylor. As we’ve seen, he is still capable of being a competent short-term option.

Offensive Line

As noted, the Packers gave up four sacks on Sunday, and they also averaged just 3.1 yards per rush, but the more alarming number was 15 quarterback hits. The Vikings blitzed more than any other team in the league in week one, though. However, at the same time, Green Bay left more extra blockers in to pass protect.

The main issue was probably the fact that undrafted rookie Donovan Jennings was forced to start at left guard due to an injury to Aaron Banks. He was an obvious weak link.

Banks is the Packers’ highest-paid player other than Love, but he’s not exactly lived up to that price-point, as he was very inconsistent in his first year in Green Bay last season. His return in place of Jennings will still obviously help matters, but despite his return to practice, he is still bothered by a knee issue and is not certain to play. They listed him as questionable.

The Packers’ most reliable lineman is their right tackle, Zach Bako-Bewele (who changed his name from Zach Tom in the offseason). Last year, he didn’t give up a sack in over 600 snaps. However, he already gave up his first sack of 2026 in the opener. Bako-Bewele is also listed as questionable but it seems unfathomable that he wouldn’t play.

The current left tackle is former first round pick Jordan Morgan, who started games at four different positions last season. Center Sean Rhyan is also versatile, having started last year as the right guard until Elgton Jenkins’ season-ending injury in November.

The fifth starter is another inexperienced player, as Jacob Monk is the current right guard. He started the season finale last season, but otherwise had only played six offensive snaps in his career.

Green Bay’s main backup is Anthony Belton, who started eight games last year, including the last six games of the regular season, and the wild card game.

The rest of their bench has no starting experience between them. John Williams was a seventh round rookie last year, but did not play. Travis Glover was inactive last week and rookie Jager Burton was in uniform but did not see action.

Running Backs

Green Bay’s running game suffered a blow when Josh Jacobs was placed on the exempt list due to an arrest in connection with a domestic incident. He looks set to miss 4-6 weeks based on the latest reports.

Jacobs rushed for over 900 yards and 13 touchdowns last season, so his absence will be felt. MarShawn Lloyd is currently listed as a starter but was held to 37 yards on 13 carries in the opener. The former third rounder barely played as a rookie in 2024, then missed the entire 2025 season due to injury.

Chris Brooks is back in a reserve role, while Kaleb Johnson is also on the roster but didn’t play any offensive snaps in the first game.

Pass catchers

The Packers’ leading receiver in 2025 was Romeo Doubs, but he signed a free agent deal with New England, so Green Bay will be hoping for one or more of their recent draft picks to step up.

Christian Watson and Jayden Reed were day two picks in 2022 and 2023, while Matthew Golden was a first round pick last season. Watson was the one to step up in week one as he had 147 yards and two touchdowns, including an 81-yarder.

However, the speedster Golden saw the most targets and was also effective. He put up the most productive game of his career with six catches for 95 yards.

Reed, who averaged over 800 yards in his first two seasons, and caught 14 touchdown passes, was limited to just three starts last season.

Bo Melton provides depth off the bench, but had just one catch in the opener. Skyy Moore is mostly on the team for special teams duties and undrafted rookie J. Michael Sturdivant was a healthy scratch to start the season.

At tight end, Tucker Kraft is a productive pass catcher who had 469 receiving yards and six touchdowns in just eight games last season.

They also added another veteran who Jets fans will recognize as a passing game threat in Jonnu Smith, as the Packers will employ plenty of two tight-end personnel packages.

Josh Whyle is back in a reserve role and youngster Mark Redman was added via trade in the offseason. Luke Musgrave, who started 10 games last year, is on the PUP list.

Defensive Line

The Packers operate with a 3-4 base defense and their starting linemen are listed as Karl Brooks, Javon Hargrave and Devonte Wyatt. However, it was a five-deep rotation on Sunday, also including Jonathan Ford, who started in place of Hargrave, and third round rookie Chris McClellan.

The 2022 first round pick Wyatt is probably the best known player in this group. He had four sacks in just 10 games last season.

The 33-year old Hargrave has been in concussion protocol and did not practice on Thursday, though. He’s listed as doubtful.

Green Bay did a decent job against the run in the first game, holding the Vikings to just 3.1 yards per carry.

Backups Warren Brinson and Anthony Campbell were both inactive on Sunday and Brinson has been ruled out due to a calf issue.

Linebackers

The Packers’ defensive star is edge rusher Micah Parsons. However, he got injured with four games to go in the 2025 season and the Packers haven’t won a game since. He remains on the PUP list as Green Bay tries to avoid a seventh straight loss, a stretch which includes last year’s wild card game.

With Parsons out, and both Rashan Gary and Kingsley Enagbare having departed during the offseason, the starters are currently former first round pick Lukas Van Ness and Barryn Sorrell, who started just one game as a rookie last year.

Van Ness, who has been a disappointment, has also been in concussion protocol this week. He did practice on a limited basis all week, though, and is listed as questionable.

Fourth round rookie Dani Dennis-Sutton provides depth off the edge along with Brenton Cox Jr., who has just one career start.

The inside linebackers are Edgerrin Cooper and Zaire Franklin, who each played a full time role on Sunday. Cooper had 118 tackles as he played over 1,000 snaps last season. The 30-year old Franklin, who has had 125 or more tackles in each of the past four seasons in Indianapolis, was acquired via trade in March.

Ty’Ron Hopper, Isaiah McDuffie and Nick Niemann provide depth off the bench. McDuffie played over 550 snaps last season but only played one defensive snap in the opener. Hopper was inactive in game one.

Defensive Backs

Packers cornerback Keisean Nixon was an all-pro kick returner but he’s now also established himself as a pro bowl cornerback. Nixon broke up a team-high 17 passes last season. He did have 13 penalties, though.

The other starter on the outside was Green Bay’s top draft pick, Brandon Cisse, who was selected 52nd overall; two spots after the Jets had selected D’Angelo Ponds. In his NFL debut, the rookie got beaten for a 39-yard touchdown by Justin Jefferson, although that was only completion he gave up all day.

The starting nickel, and primary slot corner, in week one was Javon Bullard. He had two penalties against Minnesota.

Depth comes from Carrington Valentine, Benjamin St. Juste and Kamal Hadden. Valentine is likely to be the first guy off the bench based on the rotations last weekend. Hadden is the backup in the slot. St. Juste has been listed as questionable for Sunday.

At safety, Xavier McKinney and Evan Williams are the starters. McKinney had 107 tackles and 10 pass breakups last season, while Williams led the Packers with three interceptions.

Kitan Oladapo is the only reserve safety currently on the roster, although Bullard can also play there.

Special Teams

Sixth round rookie kicker Trey Smack made an immediate impact in his debut last week as he made a 59-yard field goal on the Packers’ first drive of the season. He made another two field goals but did miss an extra point.

Punter Daniel Whelan is in his third season as Green Bay’s punter. He led the league with a 51.7 gross average last season; the third highest of all time.

Moore was brought in to boost the return game and he handled punts on Sunday. Reed backs him up.

Although Moore is listed as the kickoff returner ahead of Melton, it was Melton who handled those duties in week one and he impressed with a 59-yard return. Nixon obviously has experience there too.

Melton was also the team’s primary punt gunner last season and he handled those same duties with St. Juste in week one.

The Packers gave up a 68-yard kickoff return last week, but have some productive tacklers in kick coverage. Brooks led them with 14 tackles last season, two ahead of McDuffie and Niemann.

5 Questions with Hogs Haven: Cowboys want a better defense, but the Commanders might have got one

Blogging The Boys: What were some of the best things that you saw from the Commanders in the first game versus Philadelphia that bode well for the season?

Hogs Haven: I think the first thing almost any Commanders fan would say is the performance of the defense. Last year, the Commanders had one of the worst defenses in the NFL, so they completely overhauled it in the offseason, with a new DC in Daronte Jones (who brings an attacking Flores-like scheme) and replacing over half of the starters on defense. Early returns indicate the overhaul has paid off. The defense was living in the Eagles backfield last Sunday, generating a 48.48% pressure rate on Jalen Hurts and a 24% TFL rate, both notably higher than NFL average.

BTB: Give us a rundown on a few of the new players in Washington who could make a big impact this season.

On defense, as mentioned before, over half the defensive starters this year are new to the team. I won’t go through all of them, but the standouts are LB Sonny Styles, S Nick Cross, and EDGE Odafe Oweh.Styles was drafted 7th overall and has lived up to his billing. Attack the perimeter on the ground.

item.title: Lions defense fails to deliver on Kelvin Sheppard’s offseason commitments
item.description: Kelvin Sheppard’s three defensive commitments the Detroit Lions failed to keep against the Bills.
item.content:encoded:
The Detroit Lions could not get out of their own way in an embarrassing 41-31 loss to christen the Buffalo Bills’ new Highmark Stadium.

Defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard is very direct with his players and staff when leading his defense. I think he would appreciate fair and respectful directness in return.

Dan Campbell did not mince words at half time.

The presnap penalties are infuriating for all head coaches.

But what is most infuriating to me about Thursday night’s performance was that the Lions defense failed miserably in three distinct areas of the game that second-year defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard put an emphasis on fixing this off season.

  1. Explosive plays
  2. Run defense
  3. Third-and-long situations

Three commitments from Sheppard. Three failures against the Bills.

1. Explosive plays: “unacceptable”

The first commitment for correction this off season was to reduce the high number of explosive plays the defense gave up in 2025.

“It’s the first thing we started self-scout with, and there was overlap because you go to then doing a self-scout and we’re gonna watch it again,” Sheppard said. “And when the players come in Phase Two, Phase Three, guess what? I got 105 plays, and we gonna watch them again, and when we get to training camp and we need general reminders and subtle reminders of what to do in certain situations, we gonna watch them again.”

Well, explosive plays were an issue as the Bills generated eleven explosives to the Lions five. Below is a 25-yard pass in the first quarter that simply cannot happen.

It appears Sheppard calls a Cover 3 zone, but disguises with split safeties presnap. Thomas Harper, the safety at the top of the screen, sits on the snap and is responsible for the outside-1 wide receiver in-break. We can see this with cornerback Rock Ya-Sin points this communication at the break for Harper.

Credit to the Bills, they are in a good concept to attack Cover 3 with tight end Dalton Kincaid attacking the seam. One issue that makes this completion easier for quarterback Josh Allen is that the hook zone player in that seam is defensive end DJ Wonnum while linebacker Jack Campbell replaces with the rush. As a result, Wonnum cannot get enough depth in his drop to make that seam through a tighter window.

Now, we do not know Harper’s rules and keys for the play, or whether he should have subtle awareness that the scheme called for Wonnum to drop and play the seam tighter before breaking into his responsibility. But these subtleties may be the difference between having a young Thomas Harper compared to Brian Branch. In the meantime, these are problems the Lions need to clean up on the back end.

2. Run defense: “it starts there”

“We have to get back to playing elite run defense here because to me it starts there,” Sheppard said. “So, guys are going to go in and they’ve already been told we will get back to playing elite run defense here. And it starts with the front seven. It starts when the pads come on and it starts there.”

This is the area of the game that I was most disappointed in. The Lions run a stunt up front in one of their new looks implemented this offseason. A critical element of this is that while the stunts wipe blocks and change gaps for the offensive line, linebackers must fill and replace the gaps that are moved.

Here, we see a stunt left at the snap, with defensive end Aiden Hutchinson angling inside, leaving linebacker Jack Campbell to fill the gap behind him. Again, we don’t know Jack Campbell’s responsibility in this situation per se, but here he gets sealed by the tight end as cornerback D.J. Reed is tight to the line of scrimmage responsible for spill.

Should Jack Campbell have attacked the outside shoulder of the tight end to play the gap differently and force the spill? Or did nickel safety Christian Izien fail to play the inside shoulder of his blocker to force the spill?

These issues are unacceptable.

3. Third-and-long: “the fixes are simple”

Lastly, the Lions need to play better situational football. Blown coverages on third-and-long is the fastest way to lose to an MVP-caliber quarterback.

“We were outstanding on third down, but it was actually third-and-10 plus is like, why are we in the bottom tier in the league in that category?” Sheppard said. “Why aren’t we executing? And then you turn on the tape and it’s very eye-opening to what’s happening. It sounds easy, but it is. It’s simple solutions, man.”

Simple solutions. The breakdown here is somewhere between safety Avonte Maddox and nickel cornerback Roger McCreary.

With trips receivers to the field side, Maddox breaks on the wide receiver-3 when the route breaks inside. McCreary also sits as the wide reciever-2 in the trips set continues with the vertical route.

At the end of the game, three off season commitments to fix three glaring issues from the end of the 2025 season failed to take shape.

Is there hope for the Lions defense?

The solutions are simple.

item.title: Future Broncos: 3 Prospects to Watch in Week 3 of NCAA Football Season
item.description: Here are three prospects Broncos Country should keep their eye on in Week 3 of the college football season.
item.content:encoded:
Happy Saturday, Broncos Country. Welcome to another edition of Future Broncos. A lot of you had some great insight on prospects and questions for me after last week’s installment. Feel free to keep giving your opinions on the players I discuss, as well as any other prospects that have caught your eye early on in the collegiate football season. Here are three more prospects to watch this week—all at different positions than I’ve discussed prior.

Clev Lubin — Edge Rusher — Louisville

The Broncos are beginning their 2026 regular season without multi-year starter Jonathon Cooper in the fold. Who knows when he will be back this year, and it’s anyone’s guess how things will shake out with the ongoing legal process related to his off-the-field issues that transpired this summer.

That is giving players like Jonah Elliss, Que Robinson, and Dondrea Tillman some extended reps to see how they perform. In turn, it will be helpful for the coaching staff to evaluate their future potential. Pending the outcome of Cooper’s situation and how the aforementioned trio perform, edge rusher could be in play early on for the Broncos in the 2027 NFL Draft.

One player I’m keeping tabs on is Louisville edge rusher Clev Lubin. He initially started his collegiate football career at Army in 2022 but was redshirted the entire year. The next season, he transferred to Iowa Western where he posted 55 tackles, 23.5 tackles for loss, and 11.5 sacks.

His top-notch play led him to the Sun Belt conference with Coastal Carolina for the 2024 season. He notched 44 tackles, 12 tackles for loss, and 9.5 sacks in 2024. Last season, Lubin earned third-team All-ACC honors after posting 61 tackles, 13.5 tackles for loss, and 8.5 sacks for the Cardinals defense.

So far in 2026, Lubin has been quiet with respect to sacks. However, he has continued his penchant for forced fumbles with two on the season—bringing that total to 12 in just over four seasons of play. He has totaled over 110 pressures the past 25 games which ranks third in the NCAA in that timeframe.

If Denver wants to bolster their pass rush, he is a player for them to consider. As of now, a lot of outlets have him ranked as a Top 75 player. You can catch him in action when the 23rd ranked Cardinals host the 16th ranked SMU Mustangs this afternoon on ESPN2.

KJ Duff — Wide Receiver — Rutgers

The Broncos revamped their wide receiver core this offseason making a big trade for Jaylen Waddle. However, he failed to make an impact in his first game with the Broncos, and no other receiver stood out in Denver’s woeful aerial attack on Monday Night Football versus the Kansas City Chiefs.

Courtland Sutton has had an impressive career in Denver. However, with a huge cap hit the next several seasons and only continuing to get older, there is a shot the Broncos opt to move on from him at the end of the season. I’m not sure there is anyone in the fold on their current roster who can replace him.

Sure, the Broncos are going to try and feature Pat Bryant a lot this season. Though I believe Denver can’t bank on him being the heir to Sutton. They certainly need to add to the room. That’s where Rutgers standout KJ Duff comes into play.

At 6’5” and 225 pounds, Duff boasts the physical profile Head Coach Sean Payton covets at the position. As a freshman, Duff played in thirteen games for the Scarlett Knights and came down with 27 receptions for 42 yards and 1 touchdown. Last season, he really took off and reeled in 60 receptions for 1,084 yards and 7 touchdowns.

Rutgers has struggled out the gate during their ’26 season, but Duff has been a bright spot. In their two losses, he already has 17 receptions for 333 yards and 5 touchdowns. He impresses with his contested catch ability and dominance in the red zone. He is only a junior, though the Scarlett Knights’ quarterback situation will almost have him declaring early to take his talents to the NFL.

Does that seem like something the Broncos could use for their offense moving forward? Absolutely. If he continues to dominate, I have no doubt he will merit first round consideration next April. You can catch Duff in action this afternoon when Rutgers hosts 12th ranked USC.

Greg Johnson — Offensive Lineman — Minnesota

Virtually every outlet had the Broncos’ offensive line ranked as the top, or at least near it, entering the 2026 season. Though I felt their play against the Chiefs left a lot to be desired. That made me think about what the overall future might be for the unit.

The Broncos drafted Boise State’s Kage Casey in the fourth round in the 2026 NFL Draft. Casey has the potential to be a future starter at left guard and also saw some reps during training camp at center. However, his addition to the line shouldn’t preclude Denver from making draft day investments on the offensive line in ‘27.

One prospect down the highway from me is Minnesota senior offensive lineman Greg Johnson. Johnson appeared in just two games as a freshman. Since then, has been a key cog in P.J. Fleck’s offensive line for the Golden Gophers with over 1,900 starting reps under his belt.

In 2024, Johnson was a thirteen-game starter at center. Last season, he started all thirteen games again with 11 at left guard, one at right tackle, and another at left tackle. This year, he will be manning down the left guard position for Minnesota and hopes his high level of play can make him an early round draft pick.

At 6’6” and 325 pounds, Johnson is an imposing player in the offensive trenches. He is a big reason Minnesota’s ground game has been strong. Quite simply, he is an absolute bully with elite strength to level defenders while paving the way for Minnesota’s backs. He has performed well protecting Drake Lindsey the past two seasons.

I wouldn’t be the least bit surprised if Johnson winds up being a Top 32 selection next Spring. He has positional flexibility and the talent to be a Day 1 starter on any offensive line in the NFL. You can watch him when the Golden Gophers host the Akron Zips this morning.
