item.title: Chicago Bears Week 2 Flashbacks: Grossman, Amukamara, Piñeiro, and more!
item.description: Hope aboard the Gridiron Time Machine with @iamcogs and take a trip down down Bears memory lane!
item.content:encoded:
Climb aboard the Gridiron Time Machine as we rev the engines up for another season-long trip down memory lane!

1.) 2006, Bears vs. Lions: Rex Grossman has a career day as Chicago rolls.

Coming off a 26–0 shutout of Brett Favre and the Packers in Green Bay, the Bears returned to Soldier Field in Week 2 of the 2006 season looking to prove their dominant opener was no fluke.

Rex Grossman made sure of that.

After spending much of his first three NFL seasons battling injuries, and even hearing some boos during the preseason, Grossman put together what was easily the best performance of his young career. He completed 20 of 27 passes for 289 yards, four touchdowns and no interceptions, good for a ridiculous 148.0 passer rating. Both his passing yardage and touchdown total were career highs at the time.

Chicago wasted almost no time taking control. On Detroit’s opening possession, Tank Johnson sacked Jon Kitna and knocked the ball loose, allowing Brian Urlacher to recover at the Lions’ three-yard line. Grossman immediately cashed in, finding tight end John Gilmore for a touchdown.

The defense forced another fumble on Detroit’s next possession, this time with Alex Brown stripping Kevin Jones and recovering it himself. Robbie Gould turned that takeaway into a field goal, and early in the second quarter Grossman found Bernard Berrian for a 41-yard touchdown to put Chicago ahead 17–0.

Grossman tossed two touchdowns to Gilmore, while Berrian finished with 89 receiving yards and Desmond Clark added 85 yards and a score. On the other side of the ball, things weren’t any easier for Detroit. The Bears recovered three Lions fumbles, held them to 245 total yards and sacked Kitna six times.

The 34–7 win moved Chicago to 2–0 while giving the Bears a staggering 60–7 scoring advantage through the first two games of the season.

As it turned out, that start was a pretty good indication of what was coming.

The Bears went 13–3, won the NFC North, defeated Seattle and New Orleans in the playoffs, and advanced to Super Bowl XLI.

And for at least one afternoon at Soldier Field, the phrase “Good Rex” didn’t even begin to cover it.

2.) 2018, Bears vs. Seahawks: The defense finishes the job and gives Matt Nagy his first win.

The Matt Nagy era couldn’t have started in much more painful fashion.

One week earlier, the Bears had taken a 20–0 lead at Lambeau Field, only to watch Aaron Rodgers lead the Packers all the way back for a crushing 24–23 victory.

So when the Bears returned home for a Monday Night Football matchup against Russell Wilson and the Seattle Seahawks, the message was pretty simple:

Finish.

Chicago opened the game with a 96-yard touchdown drive capped by Mitchell Trubisky’s shovel pass to Trey Burton, but the offense struggled to find much consistency afterward. Fortunately, the Bears defense didn’t need much help.

Led by their newly acquired superstar Khalil Mack, Chicago harassed Wilson all night, ultimately sacking him six times. Even after Trubisky threw interceptions on consecutive second-quarter possessions, the defense answered both mistakes by immediately forcing Seattle three-and-outs.

Trubisky finally gave the Bears some breathing room early in the fourth quarter when he connected with rookie Anthony Miller for a 10-yard touchdown, making it 17–3.

Seattle answered with a touchdown to pull within seven.

Then Prince Amukamara made the play of the night.

With 6:37 remaining, Amukamara recognized the Seahawks’ formation, jumped a pass intended for Rashaad Penny and took the interception 49 yards to the house. It was Amukamara’s first interception since 2015 and the first pick-six of his NFL career.

One possession later, Danny Trevathan blitzed Wilson, recorded his second sack of the night and forced a fumble that Leonard Floyd recovered. Trevathan finished with a team-high eight tackles, two sacks, two quarterback hits and the forced fumble, earning NFC Defensive Player of the Week honors.

Seattle managed one last touchdown with 14 seconds remaining, but Anthony Miller recovered the ensuing onside kick to seal a 24–17 Bears win.

More importantly, it gave Nagy his first regular-season victory as an NFL head coach.

After spending the previous week hearing about the collapse at Lambeau, the Bears defense finished one.

It wouldn’t be the last time that unit carried them in 2018.

3.) 2019, Bears @ Broncos: Fourth-and-15, one second left, and “Steady Eddy”

After the excitement of a 12–4 division championship season in 2018, the Bears’ 2019 campaign began with a thud.

Chicago managed just three points in a season-opening loss to Green Bay, and things weren’t looking much better offensively a week later in Denver.

Eddy Piñeiro provided almost all of Chicago’s early scoring, connecting from 40 and 52 yards to give the Bears a 6–3 halftime lead. The offense had now gone six quarters without scoring a touchdown.

That drought finally ended late in the third quarter when David Montgomery punched the ball across the goal line from one yard out, finishing an 80-yard drive in which the Bears ran the ball on all nine plays. Chicago suddenly had a 13–3 lead and appeared to have the game under control.

It didn’t last.

Denver chipped away with a field goal before Joe Flacco led the Broncos on one final drive. With 31 seconds remaining, he found Emmanuel Sanders for a seven-yard touchdown. After each team traded penalties, Broncos coach, and former Bears defensive coordinator, Vic Fangio elected to go for two.

Flacco found Sanders again.

Denver 14, Chicago 13.

After an offseason dominated by Chicago’s very public search for a kicker following the infamous end to the 2018 season, it looked as though the Bears might not even get Piñeiro a chance.

Then came fourth-and-15.

With nine seconds remaining and Chicago at its own 40, Mitchell Trubisky stepped up in the pocket and found Allen Robinson II over the middle for 25 yards. Robinson went down at the Denver 35 and the Bears managed to call their final timeout.

One second remained.

Out came Piñeiro.

From 53 yards away, he drilled it.

Bears win, 16–14.

Piñeiro finished the afternoon a perfect 3-for-3 on field goals, hitting from 40, 52 and 53 yards. His game-winner was the longest by a Bears kicker since Paul Edinger hit from 54 yards to beat Detroit in the 2000 season finale. Piñeiro was rewarded a few days later by being named NFC Special Teams Player of the Week.

Considering everything that had happened at the kicker position over the previous nine months, you couldn’t have scripted it much better.

For one glorious September afternoon in Denver, there was no kicking controversy, and no double doink.

There was just Steady Eddy.

Gary Baugher Jr. is a second year contributor to WCG, bringing football insight backed by over 16 years of experience in organized football and more than 30 years as a passionate fan of the game. You can follow him on Twitter at @iamcogs.

item.title: Aaron Rodgers expresses faith in DK Metcalf after rough Week 1
item.description: Aaron Rodgers not concerned with DK Metcalf entering Week 2
item.content:encoded:
Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers had a quality performance against the Atlanta Falcons in Week 1. Rodgers 24-40 for 221 yards and a touchdown stat line doesn’t necessarily tell the entire story, as Rodgers was consistently let down by his receivers in the contest. The veteran quarterback showed he still has the arm to make the high-quality throws he needs.

Addressing the media earlier in the week, Rodgers expressed his confidence in the team’s ability to push the ball downfield moving forward.

“Well, the whole thing can be deceiving,” Rodgers said Wednesday. “We had a PI on a third down that could have been a touchdown. We had another blatant PI on DK that wasn’t called. We had an opportunity to Roman down the field with probably PI, not called. He didn’t come up with it. I had DK in the end zone, for sure PI. He still almost made a ridiculous catch… One of those goes, two of those goes, and it’s a whole different conversation.”

While Rodgers is right that several controversial no-calls could have changed how we look at this game, wide receiver DK Metcalf had a frustrating performance. The Steelers star receiver received boos from the crowd at Acrisure Stadium after dropping a ball that hit him in the hands over the middle that would have resulted in a huge chunk gain. Metcalf was also flagged twice for offensive pass interference in the contest.

Despite a rough Week 1 performance, Rodgers is not going to shy away from targeting Metcalf moving forward.

“I’m going to keep feeding him.”

Pittsburgh’s Week 2 matchup aginst the New England patriots feels is a huge game for Metcalf, not only will he be looking to bounce back, but he could have to step up even more due to Michael Pittman Jr.‘s status being up in the air. Pittman Jr. logged consecutive DNPs on the Steelers injury report on Thursday and Friday after initially being limited on Wednesday with a foot injury. The Steelers receiver will enter the weekend with a questionable tag for Sunday’s game.

Should Pittman Jr. miss the game, this would mean extended work for second-round receiver Germie Bernard. Despite early season struggles and injuries, Rodgers seems to be showing confidence in the passing game’s ability to iron out those issues moving forward.

item.title: 4 key matchups to watch for Bengals vs. Texans
item.description: Dexter Lawrence is looking to get his first sack of the year in Houston
item.content:encoded:
The Cincinnati Bengals will travel to Houston this Sunday to take on CJ Stroud and a very talented defense on the other side of the ball.

That defense is coming off a performance in which they allowed 36 points against the Buffalo Bills. Will the Bengals do the same, or will the Texans bounce back?

Let’s take a look at some of the key matchups in this one.

Ja’Marr Chase vs. Derek Stingley

This is a matchup of two of the best players at their respective positions. These guys are familiar with one another dating back to their LSU days. Chase is coming off a game in which he had just 2 catches for 12 yards. Stingley was credited with allowing 4 catches on 6 targets that came his way. That 66.7% completion rate is much higher than his career mark of 53.4%.

With both players looking for a better performance than in Week 1, we could be in for some fireworks.

Amarius Mims vs. Will Anderson Jr.

Anderson was able to record .5 of a sack against Buffalo during week one. He is a player who has 30 sacks through his first 3 seasons in the league. He is one of the most explosive pass rushers in all of football.

Meanwhile, Amarius Mims didn’t allow a single pressure against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. Mims was tasked with going up against a talented rookie in Rueben Bain. While that was a fantastic performance, Anderson presents an even bigger challenge due to that aforementioned explosiveness.

This titanic battle could go a long way in deciding which team comes out on top this weekend. It is important to note that the Texans will move their defensive ends around. Even when Mims is not facing Anderson, he will be going up against talented pass rushers like Danielle Hunter and Jadeveon Clowney for the Texans.

Texans running backs vs. Bengals linebackers

Not a one-to-one direct matchup, but the running game of the Texans against the run defense of the young Bengals linebacker is a key matchup in this one for me. Barrett Carter looked like an improved player from his rookie season.

However, he did still record 3 missed tackles. Demetrius Knight Jr. also recorded 3 missed tackles against Tampa Bay. They did combine for 15 tackles, with Carter adding half a sack on a play that Knight scooped and scored on. Carter would then go on to force a fumble at the goal line on Baker Mayfield, which was recovered in the end zone by Bryan Cook.

The young Bengals linebackers will need to make sure they do not allow David Montgomery and Woody Marks to run wild this week. Montgomery finished Week 1 with 3 total touchdowns. He rushed for 60 yards and added another 19 receiving yards to go with it.

Woody Marks was also able to rush for 42 yards against the Bills.

Dexter Lawrence vs. Texans interior 0-line

Lawrence didn’t stuff the stat sheet in Week 1, but he was all over the revamped Bengals defense. He was second on the team with 3 pressures during the game, and should have drawn several holding penalties against the Buccaneers offensive line. One of those non-penalties was when he almost had a sack on Mayfield, before Mayfield ultimately had the ball knocked loose by Barrett Carter.

The Texans interior offensive line consists of Keylan Rutledge, Evan Brown, and Ed Ingram. Those three players will all take turns having their hands full with trying to slow down Dexter Lawrence. Lawrence’s impact will continue to free up his teammates, but I imagine Lawrence is hoping that this is the week he gets to unleash the Sexy Dexy dance for a sack celebration after coming so close during the first week.

item.title: 3-Point Stance: The Patriots most crucial to replacing A.J. Brown
item.description: Outlining New England’s path forward without its star receiver.
item.content:encoded:
Last week, the New England Patriots experienced what life would be like without A.J. Brown this season.

It was far from clean.

Brown suffered a high-ankle sprain in the third quarter of New England’s season opener against the Seattle Seahawks on Sept. 9. Once Brown left the field, the Patriots’ offensive production regressed. Despite holding a 10-0 halftime lead, New England fell after Seattle scored 13 unanswered points.

Quarterback Drake Maye struggled to push the ball downfield in the contest. The third-year signal-caller initially threw for 79 yards and one touchdown, completing 11 of his 15 attempts. Then, following Brown’s injury, Maye connected on 12 of his next 18 attempts for 99 yards and gave away three costly fourth-quarter interceptions.

Now, with the receiver landing on short-term injured reserve, he’s out for at least four games. And to add salt to the wound, NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport expects Brown to miss about six weeks of the season, which would set him up to return on Nov. 1 against the Miami Dolphins at Hard Rock Stadium.

How will the team try to fill that void until then?

Moving forward, Maye will have to operate without his No. 1 receiver and, outside of Mack Hollins, a trusted wideout like Stefon Diggs or even Kayshon Boutte. A collective effort from the offense as a whole is necessary to compensate for what will be lost.

“Any injury that you get at this point in the offseason, you kind of approach it with an all-hands-on-deck approach,” offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels said on Saturday (via WEEI). “We’ve got a lot of different skill guys who can do a lot of different things.

“There isn’t one person on our roster who can replace anybody like A.J. Brown in the middle of a game or for a stretch of the season. We’ll band together, we’ll figure out what we can do well and try to get the guys in positions to play to their strengths.”

Still, it all starts with who lines up out wide.

Romeo Doubs

Free-agent addition Romeo Doubs had a quiet opening to his career in New England during Week 1, unable to record a single catch on his three targets.

Lining up on 2nd-and-14 at his own squad’s 22-yard line, Maye rolled out to his right with the game tied at 10 apiece early in the fourth quarter. The quarterback found Doubs wide open for a first down, but the receiver turned his head early and dropped the pass. One play later, Maye threw his second turnover, leading to the Seahawks’ go-ahead field goal.

“He dropped a pass. You know what I mean? Everybody drops a pass,” head coach Mike Vrabel said about Doubs on Monday. “Everybody misses a tackle. You talk to him the same way you always talk to him. Figure out a way to make a play to help us win, and he did a lot of great things during camp, just like everybody did. And so, I know he’s excited to get back out there, get to work and to find a way to help us win.”

In training camp, Doubs also started slowly and didn’t make much of an impact throughout early practices. It wasn’t until his role changed, working the sideline and receiving more 50/50 balls, that he began stacking positive days.

But even though Vrabel seems to remain confident in the 26-year-old, another question arises as to whether he can expand his role. In the absence of Brown, Doubs may be asked to work the middle of the field, short and at the intermediate level, which he did a lot of at the start of camp.

Nonetheless, while Doubs has struggled with drops in the past, one performance doesn’t change the fact that he can be a reliable jump-ball target for Maye and excel in the red zone. In his second season with Green Bay in 2022, Doubs caught seven red zone touchdowns, ranking fourth in the NFL.

Part of the offense’s success for the time being falls on Doubs finding his footing and potentially adjusting to a larger workload.

Kyle Williams

The same goes for second-year receiver Kyle Williams, who could help replicate Brown’s ability as a deep-ball threat if his chemistry with Maye improves.

Although the pair connected on two deep-shot scores in 2025, their chemistry was largely marked by miscommunication. Moving forward, Williams has an opportunity to establish himself and earn a consistent role on the offense.

Despite a quiet season opener, Williams had a standout preseason with that responsibility, catching four passes for 129 yards and three touchdowns.

“Sure. I mean, we want to get Kyle involved,” Vrabel said on Monday when asked if Williams’ role may expand. “I’m hopeful that Kyle can find a role for us and find a way to help us, using his speed and catch-and-run opportunities like we saw last year at times, or some shot-type plays.

The Seahawks’ defense emphasized downfield coverage last week, focusing on preventing Maye’s deep opportunities, which restricted New England to the short passing game. Maye executed that approach efficiently until he “lost patience” and began forcing unnecessary deep throws.

But if the Patriots focus on the short passing game, they still need a downfield threat capable of turning any play into a touchdown. Establishing the short game opens that possibility for a deep play, as Seattle’s defense adjusts to New England’s underneath strategy.

TreVeyon Henderson

An effective run game also draws defenders closer to the line of scrimmage to allow those attempts, and with TreVeyon Henderson close to returning, he’ll be a key part of that.

Henderson sustained an ankle injury during a practice on Aug. 24 and was sidelined through the season opener. Since then, however, Henderson has been a full participant in practices this week and said Thursday that he’s “ready to go.”

Similar to Williams, Henderson is another explosive playmaker. During his rookie season in 2025, the running back forced 30 missed tackles and totaled four touchdown runs of over 50 scrimmage yards.

It’s unknown whether he’ll be more effective running between the tackles or prove reliable at picking up blitzers and earning more third-down snaps. Regardless, Henderson always has a chance to take any touch to the house.

item.title: Browns-Buccaneers fantasy and prop bets: Bet on Harold Fannin to do this
item.description: Even if the Browns’ offense was bad last week, there’s still some enticing bets to make.
item.content:encoded:
The Cleveland Browns are on the road against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Week 2 of the 2026 NFL season this Sunday, September 20, at 1:00 pm ET. The Browns are 8.5-point underdogs against the Bengals, according to FanDuel Sportsbook. Here are my favorite player prop bets from the Browns’ perspective in Week 2.

Browns vs. Buccaneers Best NFL player prop bets

Harold Fannin Over 35.5 Receiving Yards (-114)

The Bengals’ tight ends combined for 8 catches for 97 yards and 1 touchdown against the Buccaneers’ defense. Last year, Harold Fannin led the Browns in receiving, and had 36+ receiving yards in 10 of his 16 games, while averaging 6.7 targets per game. In the opener, he was targeted just 3 times. Late in the second half, he finally caught 2 passes for 21 yards, and continued to show that ability to break tackles. If the coaching staff is trying to target things that got away from them, then not getting Fannin involved should be near the top of the list. I expect Fannin to be leveraged early this week, and with the Buccaneers’ defense, he’ll get over 35.5 receiving yards.

RB Raheim Sanders Over 8.5 Rushing Yards (-114)

The rushing distribution last week saw Quinshon Judkins get 12 carries, and other running backs (Raheim Sanders) get just 1. Then, non-quarterbacks had 9 carries, between Deshaun Watson and KC Concepcion. With Dylan Sampson out for awhile, Sanders becomes the backup running back and should get a boost in stock. He also had a nice kickoff return last week and caught several passes, but I’d look for him to get 3+ carries this week too. You’d *hope* that he’d be able to gain 9+ yards with those reps.

Deshaun Watson over 175.5 yards passing (-114)

I know we don’t like to hear things like, “Deshaun Watson looked less tentative in the first game,” because we’re sick of coddling him. However, I was saying that throughout training camp. That doesn’t mean he’s also a good decision-maker, as evidenced by him throwing the same interception on the first drive last week that he threw all of camp, but he does seem a bit more sure about pulling the trigger. Good or bad, that should lead to some decent statistical days, like last week, even if the play itself is utter crap. In other words, you can be right about him sucking, but also take advantage of the eventual stat padding via the air (over 175.5 passing yards).

Jaishawn Barham didn’t have the best game in his first taste of NFL action. However, with DeMarvion Overshown on the shelf, he’ll get the start on Sunday against the Commanders.

Again, the green dot, I think gets overblown at times, basically what you’re doing, you’re repeating the call and then you’re setting the fronts and all that. And then the entire defense needs to communicate.”

Caleb Downs looking to build off NFL debut vs. Commanders – Tommy Yarrish, DallasCowboys.com

Caleb Downs was among the best defensive players on the Cowboys in their loss to the Giants in Week 1. Now, as the Commanders come to Dallas, he wants to be even better.

Cowboys first-round pick Caleb Downs rarely came off the field in his NFL debut last Sunday against the Giants, playing 60 defensive snaps and tallying seven tackles, three quarterback pressures and a sack.

On Sunday, Downs will take the field for his first game at AT&T Stadium as a Cowboy, where he’s aiming to build off his start to the year.

“Excitement, honestly,” Downs said about Sunday’s game. “It’s the best feeling to be able to play this game. There’s no really other way to feel about it then just straight joy. I’m excited to do that, and we’re excited to do what we need to do to get a win.”

Cowboys looking to avoid the wrong side of history in Sunday’s home opener – Nick Harris, Fort Worth Star-Telegram

The Cowboys will try to avoid an 0-2 start on Sunday. If not, history shows that they’ll likely be in for a long and disappointing season.

Since 1990, only 35 of 287 NFL teams that have started 0-2 have made the playoffs. Of those 35 teams, only four have lost both games to divisional opponents.

The Dallas Cowboys will look to avoid having to make that same kind of history this season, as they look to get in the win column for the first time against the Washington Commanders in the home opener on Sunday afternoon in Arlington.

item.title: Bengals vs. Texans: 5 questions with Battle Red Blog
item.description: We tap the knowledge of one of our friends over at SB Nation’s Houston Texans blog.
item.content:encoded:
The Cincinnati Bengals are getting set for a big test in Week 2 against the Houston Texans. There are concerns on the injury front for the Bengals, and the Texans are hungry to get their first win in front of a home crowd.

To help us get a lay of the land, we tapped the knowledge of Scott Barzilla over at Battle Red Blog. Here are five questions we asked him ahead of the clash.

1.) What did you see from C.J. Stroud, in terms of improvement this summer and last week? I know there has been a contract impasse between him and the Texans—does he still feel like the long-term answer?

SB: It’s always a mixed bag with Stroud. Overall, it was a really good performance, and it makes you feel good about him as a quarterback. He had a 106.5 rating and is on pace to have a 30-TD season. However, that was sandwiched by two fumbles that played a key role in the game. I don’t really blame him for the second fumble, but ball security is a huge issue.

The question for the Texans long-term is how much they want to invest in a near-franchise quarterback, considering that they have committed so many resources to their defense. $60-million quarterbacks mean you have to save elsewhere, and there is still an open question as to whether he is good enough to elevate a flawed roster the same way the other elite quarterbacks do.

As I sit here, I don’t know what the long-term answer is. He is certainly as good as many of the quarterbacks that have gotten paid, but he is not as good as others (say Joe Burrow), so it makes it an impossibly complicated question.

2.) Talk about the loss of Henry To’oTo’o this week, and its potential impact on this game.

SB: I’m really worried that this team is already losing key starters to injury when the defense was very healthy last year. It is not as acute as when facing more mobile quarterbacks, but it still presents coverage issues because the Texans already have difficulties covering tight ends, and that is one more option taken away from them.

I would bet pretty heavily on the over for Mike Gesecki receiving yards, as the Texans really don’t have a good answer for him with injuries they have already suffered to their linebacking core (they lost E.J. Speed in training camp).

3.) Much like the Bengals, questions about the Texans’ offensive line have been prevalent. They have made moves to remedy that—did it show up last week?

SB: Keelan Rutledge may have been the steal of the draft. He was the only lineman to have a 70+ PFF rating last week at left guard. They are marginally better at center with Evan Brown than they were last season. The rest of the line is the same.

In particular, the right side of their line struggled against Buffalo as Trent Brown and Ed Ingram got beat on some key plays. Ingram was solid last season, so we can hope that was a one-off. Brown was solid down the stretch, but there is very little chance he makes it through 17 games healthy.

They signed Braden Smith in the offseason, and he is out with a plantar fasciitis injury. Hopefully, he will be able to return by week five, but that is the state of the line. So, overall they are improved, but there are still some holes that opponents can exploit. 

4.) Who are a couple of X-Factors (maybe under-the-radar guys who could surprise) on Houston’s offense and defense for you this week?

SB: On offense, the big key on Sunday will be the receiving core with Nico Collins out. Keyshon Boutte was acquired right before the end of the preseason, so he is probably still learning the playbook, but he is capable of making a big play or two.

The rest will likely rest on their tight ends and Xavier Hutchinson. I like Jaylin Noel in the open field if they give him a screen or two, but the overall production from the receivers will be an issue. A deep cut could be Marlin Klein, their second-round pick. He has a ton of athleticism for a tight end, but is still raw. If he is guarded one-on-one by a linebacker or safety, it could be a mismatch.

5.) The line has hovered between 2.5-3-points in favor of the Texans, per FanDuel this week. What are your thoughts on that and how do you see this playing out?

SB: I’m not comfortable going either way on this line. I just don’t have a good feel for the game. Like you, I think the over is as good a bet as could be had in this game. Both offenses can put points on the board, so someone is going off in this game. If you held a gun to my head, I would pick the Bengals and take the points. I am not touching this money line with a forty-foot pole on either side. I just don’t have a good feel for it, to tell you the truth.

Our thanks to Scott Barzilla for the chat. Check out the other side of the conversation at Battle Red Blog.

item.title: September is unkind to Sean Payton-led teams
item.description: Sean Payton is a historically sub-.500 coach in September. Not the best data to dig up this morning, but it is what it is.
item.content:encoded:
As bad as it was last Monday, the Denver Broncos season is far from over. And, frankly, it might just be a Sean Payton type September again in 2026.

Since coming to Denver in 2023, he has led the Broncos to a 52-32 overall record in the regular season. In September, however, he is a woeful 4-8 in that span — well below his .615 win percentage here in Denver. Even in his last four season with the New Orleans Saints it wasn’t pretty in September. Despite going 13-3, 13-3, 12-4, and 9-8 in those seasons, the team still lost five games in September.

It gets even worse when the team is average or slightly above average. The previous four years before that good run the Saints had a run of mediocrity. The team went 7-9 for three straight seasons before an 11-5 playoff season. In that four year span, the Saints were 2-12 during the month of September. Woof.

For whatever reason, Payton-led teams stumble out of the gates in most seasons. The best seasons he puts on record still has at least one early loss. Last season, Denver started 1-2. Maybe more of the same this season?

Hopefully the win comes first, because an 0-2 start would not be ideal. I’m already looking forward to October, though, given the data I just reviewed here today.

item.title: Chauncey Golston is under-sized, but plays big role on Giants’ defensive line
item.description: Golston emerging as big part of Giants’ interior defensive line.
item.content:encoded:
Chauncey Golston would like to clear something up. The New York Giants veteran defensive lineman is not, and never has been, a stand-up edge defender.

“I played the edge, but stand-up? It’s always funny to hear that,” Golston said while sitting at his corner locker in the Giants’ makeshift locker room this week. “I never played stand-up.”

Why the misconception?

“I’m classified as an edge guy. And you really just go off of what you’re classified as,” Golston said. “It all depends on what defense you’re in. Like, if you’re in a 4-3 and it says defensive end, you’re just an edge guy. But then you go to 3-4, and then it says defensive end, and you can be Cam Hayward.

“It’s very multiple. It’s all depending on where you’re playing at. And then for me, being a guy that’s smaller, I guess it just stands out more.”

In the second season of a three-year, $18 million free agent deal he signed with the Giants, Golston has emerged as a key part of the Giants’ defensive line. Generally, Golston is playing some form of defensive end when the Giants are aligned with three down linemen.

The 28-year-old played 28 snaps in Week 1 vs. the Dallas Cowboys. Via Pro Football Focus, the breakdown was as follows:

  • DLT (9 snaps)
  • DRT (3)
  • LE (8)
  • LEO (1)
  • RE (4)
  • REO (3)

Amazingly, Golston is fighting guards, tackles, tight ends, and double teams at just 265 pounds.

“I don’t have the ability to be like I can just roll out there and be big and I can take on two people. I can’t do that,” Golston said. “If I don’t come technique first, then I’m going to be out there, and it’s just going to look like Michael Oher in ‘The Blind Side’. I can’t have that.”

Golston weighed 285 pounds when he played for the Dallas Cowboys, but lost the weight last season because the Giants were not asking him to play inside.

“For what I did last year, I didn’t really ever go inside last year. So it was like, what do I need to be 285 for?,” Golston said.

Defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson pointed to Golston understanding the physical gifts he does possess, and having consistent technique.

“He’s not a big guy, but he plays big,” Wilson said. “He uses his length, his arm length. He plays with good center of gravity. He gets good vertical knockback. When you watch him, his technique is always the same. He plays same foot, same shoulder. He squeezes and constricts blocks. He plays the way that you’re supposed to play when you’re in that position. And he’s done it in the past. It’s not like he hasn’t done it. And Chauncey, man, kudos to him. He’s a guy that’s playing a five-technique in our base front. He moves around. He has a lot on his plate, but he’s doing a great job for this defense.”

Golston’s primary physical gift is his long arms. He has 34¾-inch arms that put him in the 87th percentile, and a 96th percentile 84⅜-inch wingspan.

“I have longer arms than the guards. I’m quicker than them,” Golston said. “I know how to work off the people around me. Those are some of the things that really help me when I’m in there.”

The six-year veteran says it also helps that “I’ve been doing that for a while now.”

“The overall amount of reps that I’ve had in my career because I also did that in Dallas … this is familiar territory,” Golston said. “With me playing end, a lot of it is I usually can feel what the scheme is. I can usually feel when it’s power because everything’s going fast this way, but then I see something flashing back that way, usually indicating that it’s something that the run is trying to hit outside of me. It’s little things that I’m able to pick up on because I play on the edge and I also play in there that just help me.”

Golston was on some winning teams earlier in his career with the Cowboys, and says “you can always feel the energy” when a team is good.

“Winning is contagious,” Golston said. “Not just winning the game, but just having a winning attitude overall, attacking everything, attacking the process. I really feel that. You can feel it, you can see it, and that’s really cool to be a part of. And, to be able to play my own part in it.

“And be able to help the people that are coming after me. That are coming up under me. Being able to tell them the little that I do know. And watch them take that and excel.”

item.title: Trade pickup Jaylen Reed showing positive strides since Patriots arrival
item.description: Acquired in the Kayshon Boutte trade, the safety was used exclusively on special teams in his Patriots debut.
item.content:encoded:
Jaylen Reed’s first game as a member of the New England Patriots was relatively quiet. The team, however, is not concerned about its late-summer trade pickup.

As secondary coach Scott Booker explained earlier this week, the team is happy with Reed’s projection since his arrival.

“I think he’s doing a good job,” Booker said. “First and foremost, it’s always just one of those things where you’re getting to know someone personally. When they come in the room, just trying to figure out where they’re from, where I’m from, and just trying to get a little bit of a personal relationship. Then the next thing is trying to translate what they’re defense were, where they came from, into our defensive language. That takes a couple of days. We got through those times.”

Booker went on to outline the Patriots’ developmental plan for Reed. Starting in the classroom, he was later introduced to New England’s new virtual reality room and the in-practice reality.

That progression apparently went well so far, even though Reed is still getting used to the intricacies of being with a new team.

“He continued to improve and continued to learn,” Booker said. “The details are continuing to come to light every practice, every rep that he gets. So, excited about getting him here first off, and then also just continuing to see his progression. Each program of each 32 NFL teams does things a little bit differently. It goes to stuff in the building. Where’s the training room? How does the training room work? The cafeteria? All that type of stuff. Meetings and then also on the field.

“So, just continuing to try and help him acclimate to how we do things, the communication of our safeties, the disguises and all those things that we do. He’s doing a good job and excited about him.”

Coming off a four-year career at Penn State, Reed originally entered the NFL as a sixth-round draft pick with the Houston Texans. Knee and arm injuries limited him to nine games during his rookie campaign, but he started both of the Texans’s playoff games while being on the field for a combined 82% of their defensive snaps.

The Patriots apparently liked what they saw from the 23-year-old, and brought him aboard in exchange for wide receiver Kayshon Boutte in late August. In his debut with the team, he played eight of 22 kicking game snaps and none on defense.

Still, Booker and the Patriots like his potential within their defense.

“Like any position and like anybody, the more you can do the better,” he said. “With our safeties and our corners, guys that are on the roster, having the knowledge of multiple positions if you’re able to is best. First of all, it allows you to get onto the field potentially quicker and it also helps you holistically understand, ‘Okay, if this position is doing this, then I have to do this. This is how the puzzle pieces fit.’

“We teach in a holistic way and feel like Jaylen may have some multiple-position ability. And so [we are] teaching him potentially a couple positions.”

item.title: DeForest Buckner: Colts didn't play up to our standards, whatsoever
item.description: The Colts' defense gave up 304 passing yards and 202 rushing yards in their Week 1 loss to the Ravens, and Colts defensive tackle DeForest Buckner says it was unacceptable.
item.content:encoded:
The Colts' defense gave up 304 passing yards and 202 rushing yards in their Week 1 loss to the Ravens, and Colts defensive tackle DeForest Buckner says it was unacceptable.

"We didn't play to our standard at all whatsoever, and we know we're better than that and what we put on tape," Buckner said, via JJ Stankevitz of Colts.com. "But obviously, you're only as good as your last game and that's what we put on tape. So we got to continue to prove to ourselves and prove to everybody else that we're a better defense than that."

The Colts are 6.5-point underdogs at Kansas City on Sunday night, and they know they need to play a lot better, or else Patrick Mahomes and Kenneth Walker can put up the same kinds of numbers that Lamar Jackson and Derrick Henry did. Colts head coach Shane Steichen said he's emphasizing not letting Walker break tackles.

"The big thing is tackling, right? That's the biggest thing," Steichen said. "You got to get this guy on the ground. He runs low, he runs hard, and then our run fits have got to be great."

If the Colts' defense again doesn't play up to its standards, it could be an ugly night against the Chiefs.

item.title: Patriots defense expects challenge from Steelers’ ‘conflict piece’
item.description: Big-bodied Darnell Washington could be a problem for the Patriots.
item.content:encoded:
The Pittsburgh Steelers offense does not lack star power. Aaron Rodgers is a future first-ballot Hall of Famer and one of the best quarterbacks of all time, while his No. 1 wide receiver, DK Metcalf, is a two-time Pro Bowler who has averaged over 1,100 receiving yards in his first seven seasons in the NFL.

Add the likes of running back Jaylen Warren, tight end Pat Freiermuth and other highly-drafted players like OT Troy Fautanu and WR Michael Pittman Jr. and you get a competent group of players. All of them will present a challenge to the New England Patriots defense in their own right in this Sunday’s matchup between the two clubs.

Only one of them, however, was labeled a “conflict piece” by Patriots defensive coordinator Zak Kuhr: Darnell Washington.

So, how big of a challenge is the fourth-year tight end?

“A big one,” Kuhr explained. “He’s athletic. Obviously, his size and strength are no joke. He’s great in the run game, like we’ve seen on tape. He did it last year and he did it last week. He gets the ball in his hands, he can make the first one miss if you’re not [playing] great technique taking him down. He is a great piece to have. He is a conflict piece.”

Washington joined the Steelers as a third-round draft choice in 2023, and has since appeared in 53 games for the organization. Listed at 6-foot-7, 264 pounds, he is Rodgers’ tallest weapon and one of his favorites: in their one-plus seasons together, the veteran QB has targeted the fourth-year TE a combined 45 times resulting in 33 catches, 382 yards and a touchdown.

While those numbers do not necessarily catch the eye over what amounts to a 17-game span, Kuhr and the Patriots are well aware of Washington’s ability to be a problem for their defense.

“You have to play him in the run game and he’s not just like a check-down guy,” the second-year play-caller said. “He’ll run vertical, they’ll run any type of route with him. He’s got great hands and he’s a runner after the catch. He’s a piece we’re well aware of [but] as long as we play to our identity and our style, and we play within our scheme, hopefully we’re in a good spot with that.”

item.title: Eagles notebook: Willie Lampkin appreciates all the love from fans
item.description: In the latest Eagles notebook, Willie Lampkin appreciates the love, a look at explosive plays and more.
item.content:encoded:
Eagles notebook: Willie Lampkin appreciates all the love from fans originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Willie Lampkin doesn’t spent much time online.

So he might not fully understand how much Eagles fans have been rooting for him since his impressive training camp. But he now has some idea.

“I don’t know what to say. It’s cool, though,” Lampkin said this week. “I appreciate everybody for showing me love. I just want to be the best I can be so I can help this organization reach the top.”

While many fans are hoping Lampkin will get a chance to start this weekend, it seems more likely that Drew Kendall will take over for Landon Dickerson. Kendall was ahead of Lampkin all training camp. But Dickerson’s trip to IR does bump Lampkin up on the depth chart, so he’s ready to play on offense if needed.

He’s also ready to play on special teams.

Lampkin, 24, played on the kick return team for the first time in his life last Sunday against the Commanders. He was pretty surprised to learn he was on that unit when he spotted his name leaving the locker room.

“I was walking to the team room and I seen my name,” Lampkin said with a chuckle. “I just happened to glance at the paper with the 1s and 2s. I happened to glance. I’m like, ‘Is that my name on kickoff return?!’ I was like, ‘Oh this is crazy.’ So I just went to the meetings and Coach (Michael) Clay helped me, Coach Joe (Pannunzio). It’s been great. I feel good at kickoff return.”

“I think it really is a testament to Willie,” Jeremiah Trotter Jr. said. “Usually offensive linemen aren’t on that unit just because you have to be able to move out in space and have really good feet. But I think that’s a testament to his athletic ability, showing the coaches that he can do that. He’s been doing a great job.”

Because of his unique ability and size, the Eagles used him on all four of their normal kick returns as a blocker. Because there isn’t a role for Lampkin on offense, it allowed him to get his feet wet in the NFL.

“It was fun. It was very fun,” Lampkin said. “I ain’t going to lie, it’s kind of fun chasing around the little guys. It’s fun.”

Relying on explosives

The Eagles’ offensive performance wasn’t perfect in Week 1 on a down-to-down basis. They had to rely on explosive plays.

Getting those explosives on offense and preventing them on defense has always been an emphasis during the Nick Sirianni Era and that’s not changing with new offensive coordinator Sean Mannion in the building.

“We’re on the same page there and how we think of it, how we look at it, how we look at how we create them, all those different things,” Sirianni said. “Our definitions are a little different than the league or however, whatever the numbers may be, but ours are what they are for a run and for a pass and that’s what we kind of dictate everything on.”

That’s not a surprise based on Green Bay offense last year when Mannion was still on their staff. The Packers were fifth in the league in explosive plays (based on the Eagles’ criteria) with 147. Only the Bills (157), Bears (155), Patriots (155) and Rams (152) had more. (If you’re wondering, the Eagles had 128.)

While the Eagles stress explosives, it can sometimes be dangerous to live and die by them on offense. The Eagles in Week 1 had a success rate of 37.7%, which ranked 27th in the NFL last week. But they had seven explosives that bailed them out (even though they gave up seven on defense).

As a reminder, Sirianni has previously said his criteria for explosives is any run of 10+ yards and any pass of 16+ yards. That hasn’t changed.

Here’s a look at those plays from Week 1:

• Jalen Hurts pass deep right to Dontayvion Wicks for 64 yards

• Hurts pass short middle to Dallas Goedert for 43 yards, touchdown

• Saquon Barkley right guard for 42 yards

• Hurts pass deep right to DeVonta Smith for 31 yards

• Hurts scramble up middle for 22 yards

• Hurts pass deep right to Goedert for 17 yards, touchdown

• Hurts scramble right tackle for 14 yards

Beating the heat

It’s going to be hot at Nissan Stadium in Nashville on Sunday afternoon. Really hot. The forecast for Sunday afternoon in Nashville is 98 degrees with a real feel of over 100. The Eagles actually flew out on Friday in an attempt to acclimate and to have extra time between the flight and the game to hydrate. The Eagles flew down to Tampa early in September last season for the same reasons.

Nick Sirianni this week spent some time praising the Eagles’ medical and training staff.

“They have a big job this week going in and playing in the heat,” Sirianni said. “I’d say that every week is an organizational game, meaning it takes everybody to get it done, but this one even more so with all the protocols that we go through and the checklist that we go through of how to play in the heat game.”

Sirianni said they got through the checklist with head strength and conditioning coach Fernando Noriega, head athletic trainer Tom Hunkele, VP of equipment operations Greg Delimitros and senior director of team operation Dan Ryan.

Under Nick Sirianni, the Eagles have played in four games with kickoff temperatures of 85 degrees or higher. They are 3-1 in those games:

Sept. 25, 2023: at Tampa Bay, W 25-11 — 90 degrees
Sept. 24, 2024: at Tampa Bay, L 33-16 — 88 degrees
Sept. 14, 2025: at Kansas City, W 20-17 — 88 degrees
Sept. 28, 2025: at Tampa Bay, W 31-25 — 88 degrees

The hottest game on record for the Eagles came in Week 1 of the 2000 season at Texas Stadium when they boat-raced the Cowboys 41-14. The temperature was 109 degrees at kickoff.

Thank God for pickle juice.

Getting buy-in on special teams

For the most part, special teams units are primarily built with backup players. But the Eagles have been getting contributions from their stars under this regime. We saw it again in Week 1 when Jalen Carter blocked a PAT and DeVonta Smith corralled an onside kick.

Why do the Eagles have such buy-in on special teams?

“Nobody wants to go out there and put a bad performance out there or have this stigma that you’re not a team player,” special teams coordinator Michael Clay said. “I think it’s organizationally. It’s personal for them, Smitty, JC, whoever’s starting.

“Riq Woolen had an unbelievable rep on our D-stay on punt return to mitigate the gunner getting down there and let (Britain) Covey get 15 yards. Those 15 yards are huge in our eyes because you’re not starting inside the 20-yard line, inside the 10-yard line; you’re starting out the 25. It helps the offense. It’s just a whole-player perspective, organization perspective that we’re going to do anything we possibly can to help win a game.”

Leaning into Jalen’s legs

Jalen Hurts looked healthy and fast in Week 1 when he took off running. He ended up with 46 rushing yards on 7 attempts, which included a 22-yard scramble on a crucial 3rd-and-long.

But Hurts was a running against the Commanders out of necessity. All of his yards came on scrambles without a single designed run. So there might be more opportunities for Hurts to be showcased as a runner this season.

It’s something offensive coordinator Sean Mannion definitely seems open to — at least publicly.

“It’s a difference maker for sure,” Mannion said. “I know I’ve spoken about it. It’s what makes him a unique talent, really. It came to life in the game. You can just see how he can challenge defenses that way. He made a bunch of big plays with the legs. It’s certainly something that really unlocks things for us and makes him a difficult guy to defend.”

Wrong end of a viral play

In Week 1, the Eagles were on the wrong end of a play that future Hall of Fame J.J. Watt called “one of the greatest football plays I’ve ever seen.”

And it was pretty amazing.

That was Commanders safety Tyler Owens beating Darius Cooper and Jonathan Jones with stiff-arms on his way to slamming Britain Covey to the ground after a 12-yard punt return.

“Everybody gets got once in the NFL,” Eagles special teams coordinator Michael Clay said. “I’ve been around some great gunners that have gotten got. I’ve been around some vises, that have gotten got right in there, but you have to give kudos to him to make a heck of a play down the field. But it just shows the true strength and the athleticism that is around this league, regardless if it’s on your team or not. I told Covey, ‘Don’t leave the ground. The ground is your friend next time.’”

Clay said sometimes “you’ve got to tip your cap to a guy that makes a play like that.”

item.title: How Makai Lemon is staying positive after negative yards in debut
item.description: Makai Lemon had negative yards in his NFL debut but the first-round pick is trying to stay positive.
item.content:encoded:
How Makai Lemon is staying positive after negative yards in debut originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

It was not an ideal NFL debut for Eagles’ first-round pick Makai Lemon last week against the Commanders.

He now has fewer yards in the league than when he was drafted.

In the Eagles’ 24-22 win in the opener, Lemon was targeted 4 times and had 3 catches for -5 yards. The Eagles drew up a couple of screens for Lemon that were blown up and lost yardage.

“Lot to improve on,” Lemon said this week. “That’s it. Just a lot to improve on.”

It wasn’t a great start for Lemon, but it obviously wasn’t all his fault that those plays designed for him went nowhere in a hurry. But this is a first-round pick and a Biletnikoff Award winner, who is used to producing at a high level.

It makes you wonder about his confidence. But Lemon this week said that’s still high thanks to his teammates.

“Really just leaning back on the guys that you’ve worked so hard with throughout the spring, throughout training camp,” Lemon said. “The guys in our room. They just keep encouraging me, that’s given me definitely a lot of confidence. And then just going back on knowing myself, knowing what I can do and know what I can bring to the team. That’s what it is.”

Lemon, 22, missed a ton of time in the spring and then in training camp with hamstring injuries, so it wouldn’t be surprising if it takes him some time to adjust to the NFL. In the opener, he was third in the receiver rotation with 35 snaps (64%) — way ahead of Darius Cooper’s 8 snaps. We’ll see what happens in Week 2 against the Titans.

It wasn’t all bad for Lemon, who did have a key block downfield that helped Jalen Hurts scramble to move the sticks on a crucial 3rd-and-18. That kind of effort should be lauded.

But let’s be honest. The Eagles didn’t draft the 5-foot-11 Lemon for his ability as a blocker. Ideally, they’d like to see him produce and the only way that’s going to happen is if he’s able to remain confident.

“Put your head down and work and not worry about what anybody else is saying or whatever anybody else is thinking,” head coach Nick Sirianni said. “Knowing that this is the way this happens in this league, that you’re going to have highs, you’re going to have lows, you’re going to have games where you have 100 yards, you’re going to have games where you don’t have any yards or, in this particular case, -5 yards. 

“It’s about staying focused on yourself and being in the moment of where you are and not letting anything distract you from your daily work and your process throughout the week, which is easier said than done with social media and all those different things. Our job is to stay laser focused.”

Lemon in Week 1 became the first rookie first-round receiver to have negative receiving yards in a game since Kadarius Toney in 2021 and he’s just the fifth since 2000. One of those five games belongs to Eagles veteran Hollywood Brown.

Brown was a first-round pick back in 2019, but his first NFL game was very different. In his NFL debut, Brown caught 4 passes for 147 yards and 2 touchdowns. This is now Brown’s eighth NFL season and that’s still his career-high in yards.

But Brown had tough games as a rookie too and even had that negative game along the way in Week 14. And, like Lemon, Brown came from a Lincoln Riley offense and knows the adjustment to playing in the NFL isn’t easy.

So he also knows how to keep Lemon’s confidence where it needs to be.

“Tell him that it’s such a long season, especially coming from college where there’s 10 games and you’re used to getting the ball a lot,” Brown said. “Just take it one game at a time, knowing that each week is going to look different in the NFL. It’s just staying positive and getting into your process more than worrying about the results.”

Even though the production wasn’t there for Lemon in his debut, he was appreciative that the coaching staff drew up plays designed to get him the ball. Sean Mannion called a couple screens for Lemon and even though they didn’t work, it doesn’t mean they won’t in the future.

Lemon just wants to be ready to capitalize if and when those opportunities come again.

“I think it comes down to just your process,” veteran QB Andy Dalton said. “You’re learning new stuff every week and experiencing new things. I think the biggest thing is just that you stick to your process and make sure you know exactly what you need to do, be in the right spot. For a guy like him, the ball’s going to find him. It’s going to come. So you can’t get impatient with it.”

Sirianni on Friday also stressed the process. He said focus is important when there’s a bad game or a great one.

The Eagles would love to have that latter problem.

“You need to be mentally tough enough to handle the highs and lows of the season,” Sirianni said, “because they’re there and they’re going to happen and there’s no avoiding it. I think that’s a great challenge. I also know that I believe deep in my heart, and I know that our guys on our football team do as well, that if you allow adversity to be beneficial for you, it will be.”

item.title: Roob's Random Observations: What do the Eagles need to fix immediately?
item.description: How the Eagles messed up the Landon Dickerson situation, why Makai Lemon isn't NFL ready and more in this edition of Roob's Obs.
item.content:encoded:
Roob's Random Observations: What do the Eagles need to fix immediately? originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

What needs fixing the most? Validation for Nick Sirianni’s training camp methods. And how the Eagles messed up the Landon Dickerson situation.

That all seems like a good starting point for this week’s bundle of Roob’s 10 Random Eagles Observations!

Hang on tight, here we go!!!

UNLOCKING THE RUNNING GAME: Priority No. 1 right now for the Eagles needs to be figuring out the running game and creating some lanes for Saquon Barkley. Because without an authoritative running game, this offense just isn’t going to be able to function at a consistently high level. The Eagles did run for 136 yards in the opener Sunday, but more than a third of that – 46 yards – came courtesy of Jalen Hurts scrambles. Barkley’s 42-yard run was huge, but the 17 other running back carries averaged just 2.8 yards and almost half of them – 8 of 17 – went for two yards or less. Barkley’s four carries for negative yards were the most in the NFL in Week 1. Only three teams had fewer rushing first downs than the Eagles’ four, and that’s not a particularly good Washington run defense. Barkley looks fast and strong and had a very good summer, but even the best backs in the NFL can’t make plays if there’s nowhere to run, and the run blocking in the opener looked ominously similar to 2025. Obviously, a big part of that was Landon Dickerson’s condition. When your left guard can’t move, it’s going to be hard to put together much of a running game. This is a different style of run blocking that requires the linemen to get out and move laterally and Dickerson couldn’t move at all. So Sunday in Tennessee will be a good test of where the running game is with a healthy and mobile left guard. Breece Hall ran for 102 yards and 4.6 yards per carry against the Titans in the opener, and Hall is a good back, but he’s no Saquon. Barkley is a superman, but he can’t do it by himself. I’d like to see him get 20 carries Sunday and see what that looks like. Against this team, it should look like at least 120 yards. 

HOW BAD ARE THE TITANS? Here’s what the Eagles are up against Sunday: The Titans lost to the Jets at home by two touchdowns last week, they’re 9-36 in their last 45 games and they’ve lost 14 consecutive games against teams with a winning record going back to a 32-27 win in Houston in 2024. They’re 1-19 in their last 20 games vs. teams with a winning record and they’ve lost 13 straight games against NFC teams with a winning record going back to a 20-17 win over the 49ers in Nashville late in 2021. Their 19-50 record since the start of 2022 is worst in the NFL. They’re one of seven NFL teams that hasn’t reached the postseason since 2021. They haven’t won back-to-back games since 2022 and their 7-26 home record since the middle of 2022 is also worst in the NFL. They are really, really bad and they have been for a while.

LOOKING FOR THAT FIRST WIN: The Eagles are 0-3 all-time at Nissan Stadium in Nashville, losing 27-24 in 2002, 37-19 in 2010 and 26-23 in overtime in 2018. Their last road win over the Titans franchise was 13-6 against the Oilers in 1991 in the House of Pain Game on a Monday night at the Astrodome. The Oilers believed they were the toughest and most physical team in the league and called the Astrodome the House of Pain. But the Eagles, with Wes Hopkins, Andre Waters and Seth Joyner laying out Oilers Run-and-Shoot WRs left and right, proved themselves the tougher of the two teams, leading Jerome Brown post-game to say, “They brought the house, we brought the pain.” Jim McMahon got knocked out of that game early and it was recent acquisition Jeff Kemp who threw the game-winning touchdown to Keith Jackson. The only other current stadium where the Eagles have played more than one game and are winless is the Steelers’ Heinz Field (now called Acrisure Stadium), where they are also 0-3 with losses in 2004, 2012 and 2020. 

KEEP YOUR EYE ON THE QUARTERBACK: If it seems like more quarterbacks than ever are using their legs to make plays, you are right. Ten quarterbacks had at least five carries and a 5.5 average in Week 1, and that’s the most ever in Week 1 of any NFL season and ties the most in any week. In Week 9 of 2022 there were also 10.

VALIDATION FOR SIRIANNI: Another opening-day win and another September win is continued validation that Nick Sirianni’s training camp method works. That means no tackling to the ground, shorter but intense practices, lots of conditioning, regular days off or walkthrough days and an emphasis on film study and classroom work. The Eagles are not only 6-0 on opening day, they’re a remarkable 14-4 in September under Sirianni, which was tied with the Bills after Week 1 for best in the NFL since 2021 (the Bills improved to 15-4 in September on Thursday). The only better 18-game September stretch in Eagles history was a 15-3 record spanning September games from 1978 through 1983. I know some people want the Eagles to beat the crap out of each other in training camp and hold brutal three-hour practices in the blazing heat. But it’s pretty clear that there are better ways to get a team prepared for the season, and Sirianni’s record proves it.

DALLAS CLIMBING ALL-TIME LISTS: Dallas Goedert is putting together quite a career body of work and is now one of only 10 tight ends in NFL history with at least 4,700 receiving yards, 400 catches and 37 touchdowns in his first 109 career games. If you factor in his postseason stats – 56-for-595-6 – he’s third in Eagles history with 469 catches, 11th with 5,348 yards and seventh with 42 touchdowns. He needs 21 yards to pass A.J. Brown and move into the top-10 in Eagles history in yards and 54 to pass Bobby Walston and move into ninth. He’s also within range of Tommy McDonald (5,589) so reasonably could be eighth within a few weeks. 

JALEN HURTS STAT OF THE WEEK: With his three passing touchdowns Sunday, Jalen Hurts now has 175 combined rushing and passing TDs in his first 83 career starts. Only five quarterbacks in NFL history have had more in their first 83 starts: Patrick Mahomes (211), Aaron Rodgers (198), Josh Allen (195), Dan Marino (192) and Andrew Luck (180). Hurts is 58-25 in those 83 starts, and only six quarterbacks won more of their first 83 starts: Mahomes (66), Roger Staubach (62), Tom Brady (62), Ken Stabler (61), Lamar Jackson (61) and Daryle Lamonica (60).

GET MAKAI LEMON OUTTA THERE: Not saying Makai Lemon is a bust. Way too early for that kind of talk. But he just doesn’t seem to be in a place right now where he’s confident enough in himself and comfortable enough in this offense to make plays to help the Eagles win football games. The Eagles have a pretty good slot option in Elijah Moore, who averaged 50 catches for over 500 yards per season from 2021 through 2024 and is coming off a solid training camp. Moore isn’t a superstar, but he’s a proven NFL veteran who looked good in this offense while Lemon was sitting out camp with a hamstring injury. Why Lemon played 35 offensive snaps Sunday while Moore was inactive, I don’t understand. Lemon had four targets for negative-five yards Sunday, becoming the sixth NFL WR since 1977, as far back as target totals are available on Stathead, to have at least four targets for negative five yards or less. He’s the second WR since 1977 with negative-five or fewer yards in his NFL debut, following Brandon Banks of Washington in 2010. And he’s the first 1st-round WR with negative-5 or fewer yards in a game since Jalen Reagor had minus-6 against the Chargers in 2021. He’s also the first 1st-round WR ever with minus-5 or fewer yards in his NFL debut. He just doesn’t look ready. The Eagles seem committed to getting him going and maybe he’ll start turning things around Sunday against a bad Titans team. But the guy I saw out there against Washington just didn’t look NFL ready.

HOW THE EAGLES BOTCHED THE LANDON DICKERSON SITUATION: I admire Landon Dickerson’s toughness and desire to play every snap of every game, no matter how much he’s hurting. What I don’t get about this whole situation is why he was allowed to play against the Commanders in the first place. Dickerson said in his WIP interview on Monday evening that he suffered that bone bruise in his knee a few weeks ago at a training camp practice, so I don’t get how the coaches and trainers couldn’t be aware how much he was hurting. And how much his play would be compromised. Watching Dickerson Sunday was tough. This is a three-time Pro Bowler who just couldn’t function and didn’t belong anywhere near a football field, and he would be the first one to tell you that. “I played like bleep,” he said, calling himself “a liability.” And that really compromised what the offense was able to do. The Eagles overcame it, mainly because Jalen Hurts played out of his mind despite being under constant pressure. But Dickerson should not have been out there. And if the coaches and trainers were genuinely unaware how badly Dickerson was hurting before the game, it was clear to everybody in the first quarter and they should have gotten Drew Kendall in there immediately. If we could see it, how could they not see it? I get that you don’t want to embarrass a guy who’s meant so much to this team over the last five years and yank him in the middle of the game. But Nick Sirianni’s biggest responsibility is to give the Eagles the best possible chance to win and playing Dickerson Sunday did not do that.

IT WASN’T JUST LANDON: It would be a mistake to assume that just replacing Dickerson at left guard is going to instantly fix all the Eagles’ protection issues. None of the interior linemen played well against Washington, and while tackles Lane Johnson and Jordan Mailata were fine, that middle of the o-line remains a concern. Out of 58 guards who played at least 50 snaps in Week 1, Tyler Steen and Dickerson ranked 29th and 58th in Pro Football Focus rankings and Cam Jurgens ranked 18th among 32 centers. (Out of 64 offensive tackles who played 50 snaps, Johnson ranked sixth and Mailata 13th). The o-line is supposed to be one of the best in the league and they sure weren’t in Week 1. This is a new world with Chris Kuper coaching the offensive line and he’s facing quite a challenge moving forward here trying to get this group to play up to expectations.

item.title: Eagles at Titans predictions for Week 2 of 2026 NFL season
item.description: Here are our predictions for Eagles-Titans in Week 2 of the 2026 NFL season.
