Eagles at Titans predictions for Week 2 of 2026 NFL season originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Eagles (1-0) are traveling to Nashville to play the Tennessee Titans (0-1) at 1 p.m. on Sunday.

Here are our predictions:

Reuben Frank (1-0)

The schedule is going to get much harder starting next week when the Eagles begin a stretch against the Bears in Chicago, the Rams at the Linc and the Jaguars in London. So getting the lowly Titans in Week 2 is perfect timing for the Eagles, who should – and better – get out of Nashville 2-0. This is a terrible Titans team that opened the season with a two-touchdown home loss to a Jets team that hadn’t won a road game by two touchdowns in three years. Perfect chance for the Eagles to fix what didn’t go well in their opener – pass rush, running game, pass protection, run defense – against a team they should dominate. The Titans are 9-36 in their last 45 games and the Eagles need to take advantage of this opportunity and blow this team out and get themselves to 2-0 before things get tougher. 

Eagles 30, Titans 17

Dave Zangaro (1-0)

The Eagles are big road favorites this weekend and they need to go down to Nashville and take care of business. This is one of those games the Eagles need to win and it would be nice if they didn’t let an inferior team hang around. If they have two too-close-for-comfort wins, they’d be 2-0 but there would probably be some serious questions about this team going forward.

With that said, I don’t think this game is going to be particularly close. The Titans just lost to the Jets by two touchdowns and are coming off a three-win season in 2025. I really don’t think they’re going to be much better in 2026. Cam Ward is talented but hasn’t been able to put it together and as nice as it probably was for him to get the No. 4 overall pick, Carnell Tate, in the building, it’s not going to change this team overnight. Their overall weapons aren’t great and that offensive line might not be able to hold up against the Eagles’ DL. I know, I know. We said that last week, but this is another opportunity for the Eagles’ pass rush to thrive.

On the other side of the ball, the Eagles will have to help out the interior of their line as they face All-Pro Jeffery Simmons. But a healthy Drew Kendall gives the Eagles a much better shot than a clearly hampered Landon Dickerson. As long as Simmons doesn’t wreck the game, the Eagles should be able to move the football on the ground and through the air.

Eagles 24, Titans 10

Barrett Brooks (1-0)

I’m looking for run production on the offensive side of the ball. There were times when I saw the new scheme take an L because it is so new to the line. The new run scheme is based heavily on zone blocking. I like to call it track blocking. The Eagles’ O-line has previously been in a man blocking scheme. Now they must block a space and when someone enters the space, latch on and block that defender. I know it was disappointing in Week 1, but I see how good this scheme can be for the offense. There are little adjustments and tweaks that will lead to great runs and make the play-action game a viable option. 

The defense at times looked amazing. I know everyone is harping on the sack production, but the defensive ends actually had a better game than statistics showed. I believe the edge rushers were told to stay in their rush lanes and mush Rush QB Jayden Daniels. He is such a good scrambler that the ends would have to rush through the OTs, instead of trying to beat them around the hump. The ends had to collapse around the QB and keep Daniels in the pocket.

I said all that to say: the Eagles should manhandle the Titans. The Titans are in the middle of a rebuild. The Eagles are still in position to go deep into the playoffs. They must not play to the level of any of their opponents. The Eagles must set the gold standard from this point forward. 

Eagles 31, Titans 12

Mike Mulhern (1-0)

The Eagles have never won in their three previous trips to Nashville, and it’ll be a scorcher on Sunday with near-100 degree temperatures. Thankfully, they face a Titans team lacking in talent that just got run over by the Jets. The brain trust of Robert Saleh and Brian Daboll led a pair of New York football franchises into the ground, then went out and acquired all the former Jets and Giants they could. That’s not exactly a recipe for success. 

In the end, it comes down to 2025 first overall pick Cam Ward. It’s been a disappointing start to his career. He was the 40th-rated passer as a rookie and matched that 80.2 rating in their Week 1 loss. He’s also lacked the flashes of “wow” moments fans can cling to for hope. Vic Fangio’s defense should feast on the young signal caller.

Expect an improved run game with the injured Landon Dickerson being replaced in the starting lineup by (presumably) Drew Kendall. The Eagles shouldn’t need Jalen Hurts to save them this Sunday. He can simply “play QB” and they should walk away with an easy win.

Eagles 27, Titans 13

Ashlyn Sullivan (1-0)

I don’t think this game is as much of a cakewalk as everyone thinks it is. I could see the Eagles offense especially coming out slow and this being a closer game than we imagined, at least in the first half. The one strength of the Titans matches up with the biggest weakness the Eagles have right now: the uncertainty on the offensive line with guard Landon Dickerson being placed on IR. Titans interior defensive lineman Jeffrey Simmons is one of the best defensive tackles in the NFL, and pairing with John Franklin-Myers makes for a pretty tough matchup for the Eagles guards this week. I think this will be a big game for the Eagles defensive line and they will find the pass rush that was lacking last week. Titans quarterback Cam Ward will put the ball in danger and take some sacks — he was sacked three times alone last week. I think the Eagles offense eventually finds its footing in the second half and the Eagles advance to 2-0 on the season. 

Eagles 31, Titans 14

Ryan Fowler (1-0)

Week 2 in Nashville is the definition of a trap game. For the Eagles, a massive Week 3 showdown looms with the Chicago Bears, but the focus this week will be to not glance too far over the horizon at what’s next. Instead, it’s about handling business in the form of a Titans team that struggled mightily on either side of the ball against the Jets in Week 1.

On offense, I expect Philadelphia to execute at a high level as a unit this week. I’d like to see some more screen game and targets for Makai Lemon beyond the line of scrimmage, but this is the game where Sean Mannion’s group should control the clock with the ground game before taking their shots downfield. The operation wasn’t perfect against Washington, but this is a chance to grow as a unit, open up the playbook a bit, and take care of business early. An underwhelming front seven (8 total pressures in Week 1) and a weak secondary for Tennessee sets the stage for what should be a nice day for all involved with limited push to stop the run and a lack of juice off the edge on passing downs. 

For Vic Fangio’s group, go hunt this week. Multiple sacks on the first series, force a few turnovers, heck, score a touchdown on defense. That’s my expectation for this group in Week 2. Cam Ward has all the arm talent to make every throw in the book, but his mechanics and process under center along with the correlating surroundings and structure of the offense was flat out ugly to open the year. There’s perimeter talent present in Wan’Dale Robinson and 2026 first-round WR Carnell Tate (Ohio State), but I just don’t see a path here where Ward and the Titans threaten this Eagles defense other than a few plays here and there and a possible late score in garbage time. Combine the fact that Ward is a primary pocket passer and nothing like we saw last week with Jayden Daniels’ ability to extend plays, and I expect a massive week for Jalen Carter, Jordan Davis, and Jalyx Hunt — whose seven pressures against Washington ranked 5th-most among all defenders in Week 1. 

Eagles 24, Titans 3

item.title: Three takeaways from Texas Tech’s 28-26 win over Houston
item.description: Exploring where Houston had Texas Tech’s number on Friday, and what the Red Raiders changed from Weeks 1-2.
item.content:encoded:
Week 3 of the college football season started with a bang. Friday night featured a ranked Big 12 matchup between No. 13 Texas Tech and No. 22 Houston in a potential changing of the guard game for the league.

While defending champion Texas Tech was tested and trailed the Cougars 10-0 in the first quarter, the Red Raiders responded with a 28-26 victory — stopping Houston quarterback Conner Weigman inches short of the goal line on the tying two-point conversion.

Here are three takeaways from the Friday night thriller between the two Big 12 title hopefuls:

Houston’s run game was effective but ditched too early

Houston established a rapid 10-0 lead thanks to its ability to run. The Cougars’ offensive line, led by guard Shadre Hurst, starred in the run blocking department against a retooled Texas Tech defensive line, regularly paving pathways for Makhi Hughes and Re’Shaun Sanford II. Houston relied heavily on the ground game early on, producing 61 rushing yards in the opening frame 104 by halftime. The Cougars finished with 176 yards on 37 attempts (4.8 yards per carry), and that rushing total included three sacks. Most impressively, Houston didn’t even break away an explosive run. Rather, they just chipped away at a Texas Tech defense that never allowed more than 126 rushing yards last season.

The Cougars showed the extent of their ground dominance during a 13-play, 71-yard third quarter drive, where offensive coordinator Slade Nagle carved the Texas Tech defense with 48 rushing yards. However, that drive stalled when a 3rd-and-1 handoff to Hughes on the 4-yard line was stuffed due to a missed fullback block. Then, Houston largely abandoned the run thereafter. After opening its ensuing series with a successful reverse, the Cougars called eight consecutive passing plays on their antepenultimate and penultimate drives. Both drives concluded in punts after four plays.

Winding up emptyhanded on those critical possessions cost Houston an upset bid, but it left game knowing it could control the line of scrimmage against one of the Big 12’s most formidable defensive lines.

Texas Tech finally went vertical, and Houston struggled

Texas Tech was known for its explosive passing game in 2025. The Red Raiders finished fourth in the FBS with 63 passing plays spanning at least 20 yards. Through two games this season, they only had five 20-yard pickups through the air. Perhaps it was intentional to show less offense on film prior to this Big 12 opener, but Texas Tech looked like a different ballclub and regularly made Houston pay on 10-25-yard throws.

Oregon State quarterback Braden Atkinson picked apart Houston’s defense in Week 1 on intermediate passes, finishing his FBS debut with 376 passing yards. Texas Tech followed by injecting more downfield shots into its offense this week, and Will Hammond thrived with that newfound verticality. Hammond averaged 15.1 yards per completion in his 257-yard performance, and he repeatedly found Kenny Johnson whenever he needed a big play. The Pitt transfer receiver stretched the field with four receptions for 113 yards, and he alone produced four 20+ yard catches in the contest.

Texas Tech converted 6-of-10 third downs despite an average distance of 8.1 yards per attempt. The Red Raiders regularly found gaps in the Houston secondary, which allowed them to win their seventh-straight matchup against Big 12 competition.

White changed complexion of Texas Tech defense

Texas Tech returned several starters that missed the Week 2 matchup at Oregon State, including All-Big 12 tight end Terrance Carter Jr. and free safety Brenden Jordan. However, the most essential returning piece hadn’t even played a game in a Red Raider uniform.

Last time Trey White took the field, he was donning red and black for San Diego State. The defensive end rose to stardom on the Pacific Coast as a two-time First Team All-Mountain West selection, registering 19.5 sacks and 29 tackles for loss over a two-year span. Texas Tech’s defensive line, which lost four starters to the NFL Draft this offseason, proved it was in dire need of a new lead pass rusher after the first two weeks. Still nursing a knee injury, White stepped in and made a clear difference. Texas Tech generated three sacks total, including one courtesy of the former Aztec, who regularly made Houston’s offensive line scramble in pass protection.

The rest of the pass rush stepped up as well. Miami (OH) transfer defensive end Adam Trick stripped-sacked Weigman when Houston faced a 1st-and-10 from the Texas Tech 35-yard line with a chance to go up two scores, forcing the most consequential turnover of the night. While replicating last year’s NFL-caliber defensive line won’t be easy in Lubbock, Friday night proved adding White can make this front that much more dangerous.

item.title: Winners, losers as 'backup' QB leads Texas Tech to thrilling comeback win vs. Houston
item.description: Texas Tech turned to Will Hammond for good after a disastrous first offensive play and he led the Red Raiders to a dramatic victory over Houston.
item.content:encoded:
Outplayed throughout the first half, down 10-0 after the first quarter and 17-14 at halftime, No. 12 Texas Tech secured a come-from-behind, 28-26 win against No. 23 Houston before a sold-out Galaxy Stadium home crowd.

Barely. It took a two-point conversion stop from the Red Raiders’ defense – which had just coughed up a 78-yard touchdown drive to the Conner Weigman-led Cougars offense.

Still wearing a brace on his right leg after missing almost all of the 2025 season due to injury, Red Raiders quarterback Will Hammond cemented his control of the offense in a poised effort that showcased both Hammond’s ability to read through his progressions in the passing game and flash enough mobility to uncork a 22-yard run.

Defending Big 12 Conference champion Texas Tech had an awful lot riding on this game for just the season’s third contest. The Red Raiders presently do not have another ranked foe on their schedule.

But debuting their new, signature Patrick Mahomes custom-designed all-black Adidas uniforms with electric-red trim, the Red Raiders dodged Houston’s final-minute gasp to force overtime.

Here are the winners and losers of the contest:

WINNERS

Will Hammond

Hammond technically doesn’t get the win in this game at quarterback. Why? Because Texas Tech coaches outsmarted themselves by starting Tommy Castellanos – who rewarded them with a first-snap interception on a throw-away that didn’t get away.

Completing 17 of 27 passes, Hammond threw for 257 yards and a touchdown. He added 30 rushing yards and his only turnover came when his wideout slipped to the turf and Houston’s Jalen Mayo made an acrobatic, leaping, one-handed pick.

But the gritty Hammond led two second-half touchdown drives that totaled 162 yards and that was the difference in the game.

Mack Leftwich

Texas Tech’s offensive coordinator, by his own quarterback’s postgame admission, endured a miserable week after the Red Raiders mustered just 352 yards and fumbled three times in their 35-24 win Sept. 12 at Oregon State.

And their first four offensive plays in this game resulted in an interception and minus-3 yards.

The rest of the night was a masterclass from Leftwich, Tech’s second-year offensive play-caller after a previous run at Texas State.

"I want everyone to respect Coach Leftwich, man," Hammond said postgame on the field. "He got a lot of hate this week. He went in there and dialed it up."

Of Tech’s 425 yards of offense, 241 came after the break and the unit ended the game in victory formation.

Leftwich got a passing touchdown when Hammond connected with Kenny Johnson; he also dialed up rushing scores from three different players.

His ability to continue to grow the Red Raiders’ offense and keep it multiple will dictate much of Tech’s dreams of return trips to the Big 12 Conference title game and College Football Playoff.

Conner Weigman

The rare winner in a losing effort, Weigman spent most of the night as the best player on the field.

And he was a tortilla shy of likely forcing overtime on his diving two-point conversion attempt with less than 50 seconds to play.

In Friday Night Lights fashion, Houston came up just short on its final play pic.twitter.com/EBEaiZbNdl

— FOX College Football (@CFBONFOX) September 19, 2026

Not throwing an interception, Weigman threw for 282 yards and three touchdowns on 27-for-38 passing.

He was a perfect 6-for-6 on the almost-game-tying drive. The fifth-year senior also ran the ball 13 times for 56 yards, second-best for the Cougars.

Houston outgained Tech with 458 yards and also held the ball more than seven minutes longer.

LOSERS

Houston's Big 12 title odds

The Cougars were billed by many as a potential Big 12 challenger and CFP contender.

Nothing about their performance suggests they aren’t a high-quality team.

The same cannot be said for Houston’s remaining schedule. Like Tech, Houston does not face BYU – the Big 12’s second-highest ranked team in the US LBM Coaches Poll Top 25. It faces only ranked Utah the remainder of the schedule, per the most recent poll.

Its tepid non-conference schedule, with Oregon State, FCS program Southern and next week’s foe, Georgia Southern, will do nothing to help differentiate the program in late-season.

In almost all scenarios, the Cougars must find their way to the Big 12 title game and win it to reach the CFP.

Houston's run defense

The Cougars broke up four passes, intercepted two others and even had on-the-spot coverage for Tech’s game-changing Hammond-to-Johnson completions for both a touchdown and key, one-handed sideline grab for a third-down conversion.

Stopping the run? Tech did that to itself more than the Cougars’ defense. The Red Raiders averaged 5.3 yards per carry, had four different players record a run of 11 or more yards and finished with 168 net rushing yards.

Failing to block John Curry

The real difference in this game came in the second half, when Houston moved inside Tech’s 10-yard line and trailed 21-17. The Cougars settled for a chip-shot field goal – because they couldn’t block Tech linebacker John Curry on third-and-1. Curry shot the gap, stuffed the runner in the backfield and then a fourth-down attempt became a null venture after the Cougars committed a false start – one of their seven penalties that set them back 70 yards.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Winners, losers as 'backup' QB leads Texas Tech to thrilling comeback win vs. Houston

item.content:encoded:
Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need as the New York Giants get set to fly to Los Angeles to face the Rams on Monday.

NFL Week 2 picks, predictions, schedule, odds, fantasy tips | ESPN.com

RB Cam Skattebo handled 60% of the Giants’ backfield touches in Week 1, including four red zone carries. New York ranked eighth in run block win rate (78.4%), while Los Angeles allowed 174 rushing yards in Week 1. The Rams’ Myles Garrett (knee) is sidelined, and Donald hasn’t played in over two seasons and could be limited if he returns. Skattebo has a favorable matchup and a substantial workload.

Cam Skattebo is a Giants throwback that Brandon Jacobs can appreciate | New York Post

Alone inside his hotel room, only 25 minutes away from MetLife Stadium, a jet-lagged Brandon Jacobs started excitedly yelling at the television every time Cam Skattebo crashed into a Cowboys defensive player with purpose. 

“He definitely doesn’t give a damn,” Jacobs told The Post. “His attitude shows that. Just the way he carries himself.

Believe the hype: Giants’ bully ball | Yahoo! Sports

The Giants, too, showed off their bully ball offense in the season opener, completely steamrolling the Cowboys’ defense with heavy personnel and Cam Skattebo treating every tackle attempt like an insult. Pat Ricard led the way on plenty of runs behind the Giants’ talented offensive line. Francis Mauigoa had a good showing in his first NFL action at right guard, along with the strong tackle pairing of Andrew Thomas and Jermaine Eluemunor.

I was impressed by the Giants’ auxiliary blockers at the skill positions, too. Isaiah Likely caught the passes, but the other Giants tight ends showed up to set the edge and create space for the running backs to pick their spots. And rookie Malachi Fields, one of the best blocking prospects in this year’s wide receiver class, picked up where he left off in college, providing several crack blocks on the edge and the willingness and ability to insert inside. The Giants’ Week 2 opponent, the preseason Super Bowl favorite Rams, had issues in 2025 against heavier personnel groupings. L.A. allowed 5.9 yards per play on early downs against offenses with two or fewer wide receivers.

The 10 best NFL player matchups to watch in Week 2 | PFF

New York Giants WR Malik Nabers vs. Los Angeles Rams CB Trent McDuffie. Monday night’s showdown is sneakily a big one. The Rams hope to play in much greater rhythm against a Giants team with momentum. This game incorporates several fascinating player matchups, but none better than this. Nabers made his return from an early-season torn ACL and was effective. Against Dallas, he caught six of nine targets for 69 yards, compiling a 71.0 overall PFF grade with 2.88 yards per route run.

While Los Angeles’ defense experienced a cataclysmic opener, McDuffie was the exception. In his Rams debut, McDuffie made his presence felt against both the pass and run to earn an 83.4 overall PFF grade. Given the Rams’ zone-heavy approach against the 49ers — deploying such looks on 84.6% of defensive snaps — it’s possible we’ll see Nabers rotate against both McDuffie and Jaylen Watson. Nonetheless, the snaps between these two players will be a great war.

Giants’ John Harbaugh assures benched player he is not ‘in the doghouse’ | NJ.com

Giants coach John Harbaugh benched running back Tyrone Tracy during Sunday’s season-opening win over the Cowboys. But Harbaugh isn’t giving up on Tracy. Or so Harbaugh insists.

We’ll see what happens Monday night, when the Giants visit the Rams. It’s entirely possible that Devin Singletary could continue to be the Giants’ secondary back, behind Cam Skattebo.

The view from Los Angeles

Giants’ Chris Horton: Dominic Zvada’s kickoffs are strategic, not simple | USAToday.com

Horton credited Zvada for his five kickoffs Sunday night against Dallas. The Cowboys often use one returner, and Horton said moving that player with precise placement takes skill. “He came out here, he practiced his butt off for us to put that ball in,” Horton said. “Sunday night, I mean, he was on point, and it was really good.”

The same process guides field-goal range. The staff warms Zvada up, picks a line and sticks with it unless weather intervenes. To start a game, the Giants felt good from 58 yards. Of course, he never had to attempt one. “If you’ve got to start the game, we feel good at like 58 yards,” Horton said. “This kid, he has a strong enough leg to get the ball there. But it’s all about the consistency.”

Inside the saga around Joey Porter Jr.’s future with Steelers | ESPN.com

The two sides have been here because of a significant difference between the Steelers’ view of Porter’s value and how Porter values himself. The core issue is the structure of the contract, sources told ESPN, and the Steelers’ organizational precedent that doesn’t fully guarantee a healthy portion of the contract was considered a sizable hurdle. The sides simply did not get close to bridging that guaranteed gap, which sources say made any talks about a per-year average on a deal moot. “It never even got that far,” a source said.

The Steelers could trade Porter, though the team has neither made nor received any serious inquiries about the cornerback. One NFL executive believes the Steelers could get a second-round pick in exchange for Porter and a quality Day 3 draft selection.

item.title: No. 13 Texas Tech escapes with 28-26 win over No. 22 Houston when Cougars' 2-point conversion try fails
item.description: Will Hammond is still the Red Raiders' starting QB job, leading Texas Tech to a win after Thomas Castellanos threw an interception on his first play.
item.content:encoded:
No. 13 Texas Tech escaped an upset by No. 22 Houston with a 28-26 win in its Big 12 opener at Lubbock, Texas on Friday night.

Cougars quarterback Conner Weigman hit tight end Patrick Overmyer over the middle for a 10-yard touchdown with 49 seconds remaining in regulation. Needing a 2-point conversion to tie the score, Weigman attempted a run around left end but was tackled just short of the goal line.

DENIED ❌@TexasTechFB stops Houston on the two-point conversion attempt! pic.twitter.com/KJ1pz1FO3T

— FOX College Football (@CFBONFOX) September 19, 2026

The play was reviewed, but Weigman's knee appeared to be down before he stretched the football across the line. Replay officials upheld the call on the field, ruling there was not enough evidence to overturn the play.

J'Koby Williams' 29-yard touchdown in the third quarter put the Red Raiders ahead, 21-17, finishing a comeback from an inept start and early 10-point deficit on their home field at Galaxy Stadium.

20 to the crib ✌️

📺: @CFBONFOXpic.twitter.com/RYOEacawRK

— Texas Tech Football (@TexasTechFB) September 19, 2026

The Cougars cut the deficit to 21-20 on a Jonathan Dimas field goal, but Texas Tech landed the decisive blow with an 87-yard touchdown drive in the fourth quarter that took 11 plays and ran six minutes off the clock.

Cameron Dickey finished off the long series with a 1-yard scoring run and a Stone Harrington extra point put the Red Raiders ahead, 28-20. And with that, he also extended Texas Tech's record to 12-0 when he gets a TD.

Cougars take early 10-0 lead after bad Thomas Castellanos interception

Houston began the game with a field goal on its first possession, but Texas Tech gave the ball right back. On Tech's opening play, QB Thomas Castellanos was chased from the pocket, rolled out to his right and floated a pass down the sideline that he was presumably trying to throw out of bounds. Instead, it was picked off by Will James.

Castellanos got the start on Friday, though head coach Joey McGuire confirmed that Will Hammond remains the starting QB and the team had scripted a couple plays for Castellanos at the beginning of the game.

Castellanos, a transfer from Florida State, signed with Tech in late August and he's appeared in a handful of plays in every game so far, throwing for a touchdown and running for two more, including one Friday.

Will James stays in bounds to grab the interception!@UHCougarFBpic.twitter.com/sxO4yRrfXS

— FOX College Football (@CFBONFOX) September 19, 2026

Following the turnover, the Cougars went 55 yards in 10 plays for their first touchdown. Weigman finished off the drive with a pass over the middle to Amare Thomas, who stretched over the goal line for an 11-yard score.

Down 10-0 and running just one play after Castellanos' interception, Texas Tech turned back to Hammond in at quarterback. The Red Raiders subsequently went three-and-out with Hammond throwing two incompletions.

However, after its defense forced a punt, Texas Tech got back into the game with a 75-yard touchdown drive. Hammond hit Kenny Johnson for a 28-yard gain on a third-and-12. Then, four plays later, he connected with Johnson again for 35 yards down the right sideline and into the end zone.

Air it out 🏹

📺: @CFBONFOXpic.twitter.com/K9yUF6yWsV

— Texas Tech Football (@TexasTechFB) September 19, 2026

Houston regained the lead at 17-14 before halftime on a 46-yard pass from Weigman to Koby Young, who made a spectacular catch for the touchdown.

Young trapped the ball and cradled it in his right arm before securing it with his right hand as he fell just inside the pylon.

Conner Weigman puts it RIGHT on the money for Koby Young 🤯@UHCougarFBpic.twitter.com/1hBOxGnoX3

— FOX College Football (@CFBONFOX) September 19, 2026

Houston’s Koby Young with a catch of the year candidate for the touchdown. Wowza pic.twitter.com/INp0kQvQvJ

— Bobby Football (@Rob__Paul) September 19, 2026

Weigman finished with 282 yards and 3 TDs, completing 27 of 38 passes with no interceptions. On the Cougars' final touchdown drive, he completed all six of his throws.

Overmyer grabbed 8 receptions for 72 yards and a TD, while Amare Thomas caught 7 passes for 75 yards and a score. Makhi Hughes rushed for 71 yards on 15 carries, while Weigman added 56 on the ground with 13 attempts. Houston drops to 2-1 with the defeat.

For Texas Tech (3-0), Hammond completed 17 of 27 passes for 257 yards, 1 TD and 1 INT. Kenny Johnson caught 4 of his passes for 113 yards and a score. Castellanos ran for a TD on a direct snap near the goal line in the second quarter.

Dickey rushed for 65 yards and a TD on 16 carries, while Williams joined him in the end zone and tallied 62 yards on 7 rushes.

item.title: Jerry Jones: The Giants were better than we thought they were
item.description: Jones seemingly tries to temper expectations for the 2026 Cowboys.
item.content:encoded:
The latest Cowboys' season of high expectations started with a thud on Sunday night, when Dallas lost to the Giants in the regular-season opener.

In a Friday appearance on 105.3 The Fan in Dallas, Cowboys owner and G.M. Jerry Jones acknowledged that the outcome had something to do with the opponent.

"They just did a good job all over," Jones said regarding the Giants. "And I will tell you, they were better than we thought they were. I'm anxious to see how New York continues to play, but I really — combination of things. We didn't play as well as we should play and can play, but they played better than I thought they could."

Was it also a product of the Cowboys not being as good as Jones had thought they would be?

"Of course," Jones said. "Well, and to say it that way, I'd rather say it more positively. We're not at the level that we thought we would be.

"I can give you a lot of reasons, logical reasons. We're dealing with a conceptually new coaching staff, dealing with a 'new' to a lot of people out there. The defensive scheme. And then you're dealing with people who are fresh into that scheme. Now, you got some really veteran players out there. But still, they're changing up some of the things that they're doing. Are they capable of doing what we're asking? Absolutely they are.

"But the bottom line is that the last time, frankly, the last time that, from my perspective, that we had as many changes on defense, we had as many changes with the coaching staff, had as much change with the personnel, and had as much change with the team was the first year Jimmy Johnson was our coach, and we won one football game.

"Now, things have changed, and you can come in with less experience than you could in those days. But having said that, it's a challenge now to put it together and get it ready to go. We didn't play well last week. I said — what I meant to say was, New York had really more to do with it than I thought they would. Than I thought they would. And so that's a factor. But Washington could have a lot to do with it here Sunday, too, so we've got to be ready to step up the level of play. There's no question."

It's a sensible explanation. But it cuts against the vibe that had been created before the season, when season tickets were being renewed and hype was being generated and fans were being persuaded that things would be different this year.

What should the real expectations be? With Jerry suggesting that the Cowboys undergone an overhaul they haven't experienced since the year Jones bought the team, they perhaps should be a lot lower than they were a week ago.

item.title: New York Jets: Stopping the run
item.description: A passing league no more?
item.content:encoded:
We hear it all the time. The NFL is a passing league. You have to pass the ball and defend the pass well to win in this league. Running backs don’t matter. Stopping the run is less important than stopping the pass. That’s the conventional wisdom these days, but is it true?

As it happens, the league has quietly undergone an extraordinary transformation over the last decade or so. In 2015 the league set an all time record of 244 passing yards per game. Passing offenses seemed  unstoppable. 13 NFL teams surpassed 4000 passing yards that year. Even the Jets got in on the fun, passing for 4057 yards. Everybody was trying to figure out how to slow down all the high powered passing offenses. Gradually, over the next 10 years, they largely succeeded.

Ten years later in 2025, NFL teams averaged just 210 passing yards per game, the lowest total since 2006. That represented an enormous drop of 34 passing yards per game from the peak of 2015. There has never been another ten year stretch with that level decrease in passing yards in post-merger NFL history.

Just six teams surpassed 4000 passing yards in 2025, down more than 50% from a decade earlier. The average team attempted just 32.1 passes per game in 2025, the lowest total since 2006. The last time the NFL had a substantial stretch of years where teams averaged lower than 32.1 passes per game was more than 40 years ago, in the late 1970s through the early 1980s. Back then nobody was calling the NFL a passing league. In fact, there was such a dearth in passing and scoring back then the NFL started a series of rule changes to encourage passing and scoring.

Passing efficiency has also been going through a significant decline lately. In 2025 the NFL averaged 6.09 net yards per passing attempt, down .32 net yards per attempt from the all time high of 6.41 set 10 years earlier. That level of decline in a decade has only been surpassed once in post-merger NFL history, from 1989 through 1997.

At the same time rushing yards have been increasing. Rushing yards per game hit a 16 year low in 2015 at 108.9 yards per game. There have only been four seasons in all of NFL history with less rushing yards per game. By 2024 that number had risen to 119.8 rushing yards per game, the highest number since 1988.

Rushing efficiency has also been on the rise. In 2005 teams averaged 4.0 yards per rushing attempt. By 2025 that number was up to 4.4 yards per attempt, the second highest number in NFL history, just 0.1 yards less than the record of 4.5 set in 2022.

All of this suggests that the NFL may not be as much of a passing league as common wisdom suggests. In fact, in an everything old is new again moment, the old fashioned approach of emphasizing stopping the run seems to be back in style. It’s just one week, and cause and effect are a bit tricky here, as losing teams tend to pass more and run less, but for at least one week, the teams that stopped the run excelled this season. The top ten teams in fewest rushing yards allowed have a combined record of 8-2 this season. The 1-0 Jets are one of those teams, ranking fourth in the NFL with just 68 rushing yards allowed.

We’ll see what the rest of the 2026 season has in store, but maybe Aaron Glenn and Darren Mougey were on to something in the offseason. The Jets brought in a bunch of guys who excel at stopping the run on defense. They also brought in a number of sure tacklers. Maybe we’re going back to the future. Maybe the NFL is not such a passing league after all. Maybe the Jets are in the process of building the right kind of defense for modern NFL offenses, which increasingly seem determined to run the ball. We’ll find out over the next few months, but maybe this Jets defense is about to surprise a lot of people.

item.title: Titans vs. Eagles predictions: Pain
item.description: It is going to be another tough Sunday at Nissan Stadium.
item.content:encoded:
I’d love to have a positive prediction for the Tennessee Titans in their week two matchup with the Philadelphia Eagles, but I honestly cannot come up with one. The Titans looked so bad against the New York Jets last week. The Eagles are a much better team than the Jets. There is no reason to think this week will look any different.

Hats off to any of you who are going to the game on Sunday. It is going to be 100 degrees, and the stadium is going to be mostly Eagles fans. That doesn’t sound like a fun afternoon to me.

The line is currently Titans +7 at FanDuel Sportsbook. That seems way too low to me. If I were a betting man, I’d probably take an alternate line all the way up to Eagles -10. You can probably get that one at pretty good odds.

My prediction is that the Eagles score early and often. The Titans will do basically nothing on offense through the first three quarters, but will get a touchdown in garbage time like they did last week.

Score prediction: Eagles 31 Titans 10

Can you come up with anything positive you think the Titans will be able to do in this game?

item.title: Marvin Lewis likes what he sees in the new-look Bengals defense
item.description: “They played confident.”
item.content:encoded:
The Cincinnati Bengals are getting geared up for a date with the Houston Texans this Sunday as they look to move to 2-0 on the young season. A major reason for their win in week one over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers was the play of the new-look defense for Zac Taylor and Al Golden.

Forcing four turnovers, it was a great sight for Bengals fans as they hope to see their team make a run back to the playoffs. There is still a long season to go, but the fans aren’t the only people impressed with the defense in week one. Former Bengals head coach Marvin Lewis also likes what Al Golden has going on.

On Inside Football, Lewis had this to say;

“They played confident; they stripped the football. They were going after it each and every play. Adding [Boye] Mafe from the Seahawks, Jonathan Allen, Bryan Cook, who actually was a camper at the Marvin Lewis football camp, and he reminded me that when I was there.

“Then their second-round pick, also, Cashius Howell. These dudes came through, man. The two young linebackers were not a liability on defense, and then the secondary played their tail off, and that’s what they needed.”

With impressive safety play from Jordan Battle and good pressure from a retooled defensive line, it finally looks like the team has something to work with on the defensive side of the ball.

Will that continue against the Texans? Going to be interesting to watch this Sunday.

item.title: Kyle Shanahan defends Sean McVay’s blunder on 49ers-Rams opening season in Australia
item.description: Sean McVay said he hoped the Rams wouldn’t have to play in Australia ever again. His comments immediately went viral because of the team’s decision to fly into Melbourne late...
item.content:encoded:
Sean McVay said he hoped the Rams wouldn’t have to play in Australia ever again.

His comments immediately went viral because of the team’s decision to fly into Melbourne late and the 27-7 beatdown handed to the Super Bowl favorites by the 49ers.

Kyle Shanahan was asked the same question Friday about returning to Australia, and he quickly defended McVay in his response.

“You’re really trying to get me in trouble,” Shanahan said. “It’s just, you don’t want it to come off the wrong way, how you word it. Just like Sean doesn’t want to.

“Seventeen games are very tough. Every game is so tough and what you put into it for seven days. Anytime you put more travel on it, it makes it a lot harder.

“That’s something no team really wishes for, whether it’s 16 hours away or five hours away. The farther, the harder. All international games are like that, too, with that being the farthest. That’s why you always hope it’s timed out where you can have a bye week after.”

There’s always going to be a push and pull between the business side of the NFL and the football side. Football players and coaches thrive on a routine week in and week out. When that routine is disrupted, it can make preparation for a game difficult.

On the other hand, the expansion of the sport is important, and the 49ers embraced their weeklong trip to Australia. San Francisco fulfilled its international duties and kicked off the 2026 season in dominant fashion.

Now, it’s time to see whether the 49ers will continue trending upward with a Week 2 matchup against the Dolphins.
